# ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling

Guangrui Xie ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author: guanx92@vt.edu

August 24, 2026

###### Abstract

This paper presents ORPilot, an open-source agentic AI system that
translates real-world natural-language business problems into working
and solver-ready optimization models. Unlike prior LLM-for-OR tools
created in a pure academic setting, which assume a clean and complete
problem specification with pre-formatted data embedded in problem text,
ORPilot is designed from the ground up for production conditions:
ambiguous problem descriptions, large-scale raw operational data, and
the need for reproducibility and portability across different solver
backends. The system achieves this through four novel components rarely
present in existing work: (1) a conversational interview agent that
elicits a complete problem specification before any modeling efforts
begin, (2) a data collection agent that collects data independently
instead of embedding data into prompts, (3) a parameter computation
agent that bridges the gap between raw tabular data and model-ready
parameters, and (4) a solver-agnostic Intermediate Representation (IR)
that enables deterministic, zero-LLM-call recompilation to different
solver backends (Gurobi, CPLEX, PuLP, Pyomo, or OR-Tools). Moreover,
self-correcting retry loops are introduced to feed solver errors and
tracebacks back to the LLMs for targeted repairs. To my knowledge,
ORPilot is the first-ever attempt for creating a LLM-for-OR tool that is
targeted against production-level business problems, rather than
textbook operations research (OR) problems. I evaluated ORPilot on
real-world sized problems and obtained promising results. Although
textbook OR problems are not in the comfort zone of ORPilot, I also
tested ORPilot on three traditional academic benchmarks – IndustryOR,
NL4OPT, and NLP4LP. ORPilot delivered performance superior to other
state-of-the-art LLM-for-OR tools in terms of the overall accuracy on
the industrial IndustryOR benchmark, and comparable performance on
NL4OPT and NLP4LP.

Keywords: Large Language Models, Artificial Intelligence, AI Agent,
Operations Research, Optimization Modeling, Decision Making

Code:
[https://github.com/GuangruiXieVT/ORPilot](https://github.com/GuangruiXieVT/ORPilot)

## 1 Introduction

Operations Research (OR) has long been one of the most practically
valuable disciplines in applied mathematics, underpinning decisions in
logistics, supply chain management, scheduling, finance, and beyond.
Despite decades of mature solver technologies (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX,
etc.), the barrier to building and deploying optimization models remains
high. Industry practitioners who want to solve a business problem
through optimization often lack expertise in mathematical programming,
while a well-trained OR consultant may lack domain knowledge.
Translating a real-world business problem into a mathematical
optimization model often requires iterative dialogs between a domain
expert and an OR consultant.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened a plausible path to
democratizing optimization modeling. A growing body of work, e.g.,
OptiMUS \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\], OR-LLM
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\], and others, have demonstrated that state-of-the-art
LLMs can generate correct solver code for well-specified linear
programming (LP) and mixed integer programming (MIP) problems. These
results, however, have been obtained almost exclusively in a controlled
academic setting: the problem description is complete and unambiguous,
all numerical data appear inline in the prompt, and the task reduces to
code synthesis from a mathematics textbook problem.

However, real-world OR deployments are categorically different. Industry
practitioners are barely able to describe all aspects of the business
problem they are facing in a one-go prompt. A business analyst
describing a production-planning problem will likely omit assumptions
they consider obvious, conflate decision variables with parameters, and
provide data in operational spreadsheets rather than as a neatly
formatted numerical table in the prompt. Existing LLM-for-OR tools fall
short on addressing these issues.

ORPilot is aimed at addressing this gap. It is, to my knowledge, the
first LLM-based OR tool designed explicitly for production conditions,
featuring the following architectural novelties:

1\. An interview agent that conducts a structured dialog with the user,
asking targeted clarifying questions until the problem specification is
complete and unambiguous before any modeling efforts begin.

2\. A data collection agent that instructs the user on what data to
prepare with clear schema requirements for the data tables.

3\. A parameter computation agent that inspects raw data tables (e.g.,
CSV files) the user provides, identifies what derived quantities (e.g.,
distance matrices, aggregated parameters, BigM values) the model
requires, generates and executes a Python script to compute them, and
exposes the results as additional computed data tables.

4\. A solver-agnostic Intermediate Representation (IR) – a compact,
typed JSON schema capturing sets, parameters, variables, objectives, and
constraints with references to the CSV files generated in the previous
steps as data sources. The IR decouples model formulation from
solver-specific code and enables deterministic recompilation,
reproducibility, and backend portability without further LLM calls.

These components are embedded in a self-correcting pipeline:
LLM-generated code that fails at the solver level is automatically
repaired by feeding error messages, infeasibility signals, and full
tracebacks back to the LLM for a targeted revision, up to a configurable
number of retries.

I evaluated the performance of ORPilot using three optimization problems
in the supply chain industry with real-life sized data, mirroring how an
OR consultant would perform OR modeling for business users in practice.
Although ORPilot is not designed for academic benchmarks, I also
evaluated ORPilot on three public academic benchmarks (IndustryOR
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\], NL4OPT \[[5](#bib.bib5)\], NLP4LP \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\]) and reported accuracy figures to
provide a comparison with other existing LLM-for-OR tools. On IndustryOR
(the most industrially representative benchmark), ORPilot with GPT-4o
outperforms OptiMUS-0.3 (37% accuracy \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]) with 46%
accuracy, while ORPilot with Claude-Sonnet-4.6 achieves 75% overall
accuracy on the same benchmark.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 surveys
related work. Section 3 describes the system architecture in detail.
Section 4 presents the experimental results. Finally, section 5
concludes the paper with some discussions on the experimental results
and future improvements.

## 2 Relevant Work

The application of LLMs to OR has grown rapidly into a broad field. A
recent survey paper \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] provided a systematic review
covering three research pathways: automatic modeling (translating
natural language into solver code), LLM-assisted optimization (e.g.,
heuristic generation, evolutionary algorithms), and direct solving (LLM
as black-box optimizer). ORPilot belongs to the automatic modeling
pathway and is most directly related to prompt-driven code generation
systems. Hence, the discussion in this section is organized accordingly
based on this survey paper.

### 2.1 Prompt-Driven Automatic Modeling

The dominant approach to LLM-based OR modeling is to construct a prompt
that contains the problem description and ask the LLM to generate solver
code or a mathematical formulation in a single pass or a fixed
multi-step pipeline.

The OptiMUS series \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\] is
the most developed work in this direction. The initial version OptiMUS
progressively converts natural language into a solvable optimization
model through structure generation, code generation, execution
validation and feedback correction, and introduced the NLP4LP dataset.
OptiMUS-0.2 added a connection-graph mechanism to track dependencies
between variables, constraints and parameters. The latest version,
OptiMUS-0.3, further integrated a structure detection agent and
structure pool, combined with prompt-retry and self-correction loops,
and reported 37% accuracy on the IndustryOR benchmark using GPT-4o.
Chain-of-Experts \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] proposed a multi-agent chain in
which role-specific agents handle terminology parsing, model
construction, code generation, and verification, with a two-stage
reasoning mechanism of forward construction and backward reflection.
OR-LLM-Agent \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] introduced a reasoning-driven
closed-loop framework that uses structured prompts to transform natural
language into LP models, automatically generates executable code, and
performs repairs and validations in a sandbox – the closest in spirit to
ORPilot’s retry loop. Autoformulator \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] combined
hierarchical decomposition and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with
structured templates to systematically explore alternative formulations.
NL4OPT \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] first introduced the shared task and dataset
for formulating LP problems from natural language while establishing a
standard evaluation protocol.

Beyond prompting, a parallel line of work combines structured prompts
with model fine-tuning to improve accuracy and robustness on complex
problems. ORLM \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] constructed the IndustryOR benchmark –
the most industrially representative dataset in this area, and trained
the ORLM series of fine-tuned models that outperformed GPT-4 on NL4OPT,
MAMO, and IndustryOR. LLMOPT \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] defined a unified
five-element modeling structure: sets, parameters, variables,
objectives, and constraints, and used supervised fine-tuning, model
alignment, and self-correction to significantly improve modeling
reliability. This five-element schema is structurally similar to
ORPilot’s intermediate representation (IR); however, LLMOPT uses it as a
training target for a fine-tuned LLM, whereas ORPilot uses it as an
executable IR that is compiled deterministically to solver code without
further LLM calls, enabling reproducibility and backend portability.
LLaMoCo \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] introduced code-to-code instruction tuning
with a large-scale instruction set, achieving stronger semantic
understanding and generalization in code generation for optimization
tasks. OptMATH \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] constructed high-quality triplet
datasets (natural language, mathematical expression, solver code) with
feedback-based difficulty adjustment.

All of these systems discussed above share a common assumption: the
problem description is complete and unambiguous, and all numerical data
appear inline with clean formats. ORPilot relaxes both assumptions.

### 2.2 Intermediate Representation in OR Modeling

The use of structured intermediate representations (IR) between natural
language and solver code is an emerging theme. NL2OR
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\] generated a domain-specific language (DSL) as an
intermediate step with grammar correction and JSON Schema validation
before producing solver code. EquivaMap \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] used
LLM-generated variable mappings to assess the semantic equivalence of
different formulations of the same problem on the NLP4LP dataset.

ORPilot’s IR goes further: it is a fully typed, Pydantic-validated JSON
schema that captures the complete model structure; it is compiled
deterministically to any of the five solver backends (Gurobi, CPLEX,
PuLP, Pyomo, OR-Tools) with zero LLM calls, and persists as a portable
artifact that can be archived, edited, and re-solved independently of
any LLM connection.

### 2.3 Interactive and Conversational OR Systems

OptiGuide \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] integrated GPT-4 with a supply chain
optimizer, translating user queries into optimization code modifications
and forming a closed feedback loop achieving over 90% accuracy in
Microsoft Azure deployment. However, OptiGuide assumes an existing fully
specified model. It handles what-if queries on top of a fixed
formulation rather than eliciting the formulation from scratch. OptLLM
\[[16](#bib.bib16)\] enabled multi-round conversation between the user
and the system to elicit problem specifications and handles external
data outside prompts. However, the tool still assumes model-ready data
is available and lacks an IR for reproducibility and portability.
Decision Optimization CoPilot (DOCP) \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] articulated
the research vision for conversational decision-optimization tools,
identifying problem elicitation, data handling, and reproducibility as
open challenges. ORPilot is, to my knowledge, the first concrete system
to address all these challenges.

### 2.4 Parameter Derivation from Raw Data

The gap between raw operational data and model-ready parameters has
received almost no attention in the LLM-for-OR literature.
\[[18](#bib.bib18)\] proposed an automatic MILP construction framework
for multi-robot task allocation that uses a domain knowledge base to
guide variable and constraint generation, but assumed the relevant
numerical quantities are already available. OR-LLM-Agent
\[[8](#bib.bib8)\] incorporated a validation chain but did not address
parameter transformation from raw tables.

ORPilot’s parameter computation agent is, to my knowledge, the first
component specifically designed to inspect raw tabular data, identify
what derived quantities (e.g., pairwise distance matrices, aggregated
parameters, BigM values) the model requires, generate and execute a
Python script to compute them, and pass the results as additional
structured inputs to the code generation step.

## 3 System Architecture

ORPilot is implemented as a LangGraph state machine
\[[19](#bib.bib19)\]. Each pipeline step is an independently testable
agent node. The standard pipeline of ORPilot is illustrated in Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 System Architecture ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").

The pipeline starts by the interview agent asking the user questions
about the business problem to be solved through an interactive
conversation. Once the interview agent completes the conversation with
the user, the data collection agent thinks about what data would be
needed to model this problem and gives instructions to the user on what
data to prepare and how to prepare them through an interactive
conversation. Once the data collection agent decides that all needed
data are provided in the correct format, the problem specification and
the collected data schema will be passed to the parameter computation
agent to derive any secondary parameters that are required by the
optimization model, but not readily available in the raw data the user
provided. Then the code generation agent receives the information of
problem specification, raw data tables, and derived parameter tables to
generate the code for building and solving the optimization model. The
solver code is then executed in a secured sandbox to try to find the
optimal solution. A self-correcting loop is embedded here to fix any
mistake that the code generation agent could have made when the solver
execution step returns an error or infeasible or unbounded solution. The
maximum number of retries is limited by a user-defined parameter to
prevent infinite loops. Upon successful code executions returning an
optimal solution, the solution is passed to the reporter agent to
summarize the optimization results. The reporter agent will communicate
the findings to the user in plain English. Useful artifacts can be
generated and saved along with the pipeline for later analysis the user
might need to do. These artifacts include (1) an intermediate
representation (IR) which is a structured json blob that extracts the
skeleton of this optimization problem, (2) a python file that stores the
code for generating the optimization model, (3) the lp file of this
particular optimization model and (4) a session file that stores
necessary information along with the pipeline which allows the user to
resume from the current session later if this session is interrupted.
The following subsections discuss the necessity and contribution of each
novel component of ORPilot standard pipeline independently.

![Refer to caption](2605.02728v1/regular_pipeline.png)

Figure 1: ORPilot standard pipeline. Blue indicates an LLM-involved
step, while orange indicates a deterministic step. Double arrows in
opposite directions indicate the interactive nature of this step. Solid
arrows represent unconditional transitions between steps, while dashed
arrows represent conditional transitions between steps.

### 3.1 Interview Agent

The interview agent is the entry point for end users. It receives a
free-form natural-language description of a business problem which may
be vague, incomplete, or self-contradictory and engages the user in a
structured dialog to elicit a complete problem specification.

The key design principle is that no modeling efforts should begin until
the interview is complete. This mirrors the practice of a human OR
consultant. Business users are barely able to describe the business
problems they want to model accurately enough in a single paragraph. A
good consultant will spend substantial time with business users to
understand the problem before writing a single constraint. Premature
modeling based on an underspecified problem produces models that are
technically correct but practically wrong. This design of ORPilot is
fundamentally different than previous work on LLM-for-OR tools, which
are aimed at solving textbook OR problems with clean problem
descriptions and model-ready data.

The interview agent is prompted to (a) identify information gaps in the
current description, (b) ask at most one targeted clarifying question
per turn to avoid overwhelming the user, and (c) terminate the interview
and advance the pipeline once the objective function, decision
variables, constraints, and data requirements are unambiguously
specified. The agent maintains a running structured summary of the
problem that is updated after each exchange and passed to downstream
steps. Before ending the interview, the agent would provide the user
with a summary clearly stating the objective, decision variables,
constraints, parameters and indices of each parameter. The user has the
chance to make any final corrections by communicating with the agent
before this structure summary is passed to downstream processes. Refer
to Section
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"),
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
and
[K](#A11 "Appendix K Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
for real examples of interview agent – user conversations.

### 3.2 Data Collection Agent

This step has no counterpart in any existing LLM-for-OR tool. Existing
tools are limited to accepting a single, pre-written problem text with
clean and model-ready data embedded in it. However, in practice, solving
a real-life optimization problem often requires a huge amount of data
that can hardly be directly embedded in the prompt fed to LLMs, due to
the maximum token limits. Even if the maximum token limits are not a
hurdle, combining data into the prompt will likely increase the chance
of hallucinations of LLMs. ORPilot is designed with the notion that data
should live separately from the prompt and can only be accessed by AI
agents through writing code. Hence, ORPilot adopts a data collection
agent dedicated to understand what data the user has available and
instruct the user on data preparation.

Based on the problem specification the interview agent obtained from the
user, the data collection agent determines exactly what tabular data is
required: which entities (sets) exist, what attributes (parameters) each
entity has, and what data types and semantics apply. The agent presents
this schema to the user and waits for them to supply data as CSV files
to the file path specified by the agent. It then validates the
completeness and consistency of the uploaded data before proceeding. If
the user does not have the model-ready data to satisfy the schema
specified by the agent (e.g., the agent asks for the distance between
two locations, but the user only has coordinates of the two locations),
the user can indicate this to the data collection agent, and the agent
will update the schema requirement based on what the user actually has
at hand and let the parameter computation agent compute model-ready
parameters by passing a message to it. Refer to Section
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"),
[G](#A7 "Appendix G Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
and
[L](#A12 "Appendix L Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
for real examples of data collection agent – user conversations.

### 3.3 Parameter Computation Agent

This step is perhaps the most significant departure from prior work.
Most existing LLM-for-OR tools assume that all numerical quantities
needed by the model appear directly in the problem statement or attached
data. This is essentially never true in practice. Consider two
representative examples:

1.  1.  A vehicle routing model needs a distance matrix between locations.
        The user only has city coordinates. Computing pairwise Euclidean or
        geographic distances requires a transformation step that is entirely
        outside the scope of LP/MIP formulation.
2.  2.  A multi-period production scheduling model needs aggregate demand
        per time period. The user only has a transaction ledger with one row
        per order. The model parameter is a sum-aggregation over the raw
        data.

The parameter computation agent bridges this gap. It receives the
structured problem specification from the interview agent and the raw
CSV files from the data collection agent. It then (1) identifies which
model parameters cannot be read directly from the raw tables (derived
parameters), (2) generates a Python script to compute these derived
parameters from the raw data, (3) executes the script in a sandboxed
environment, and (4) writes the results as additional CSV files, which
are passed to the code generation step.

This ensures that the code generation step always receives model-ready
parameters (clean, correctly typed, and correctly indexed, rather than
raw operational data), which results in substantially more reliable code
generation and fewer retries.

### 3.4 Code Generation and Self-Correcting Retry Loop

The code generation step receives the full problem specification and all
parameter CSV files and generates a complete Python solver script for
the chosen backend. ORPilot currently supports five backends (Gurobi,
CPLEX, PuLP, Pyomo and OR-Tools), and the generated code is
backend-specific.

The generated code is immediately executed. If the solver returns an
error (syntax error or runtime exception) or infeasibility signal or
unbounded signal, the full error message and traceback are fed back to
the LLM along with the previously generated code, and code generation is
retried. This loop runs up to $`N`$ times (configurable). In practice,
the majority of failures are resolved within one or two retries. Refer
to Section
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"),
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
and
[M](#A13 "Appendix M Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
for real examples of the code generated by the code generation agent.

### 3.5 Intermediate Representation (IR)

A central design goal of ORPilot is reproducibility and portability:
once a model has been solved successfully, it should be possible to
re-run it with a different solver backend, to perform what-if analysis
by editing the data, or to archive the model in a form that does not
depend on a live LLM connection.

To achieve this, ORPilot defines a solver-agnostic Intermediate
Representation (IR) – a compact, typed JSON schema that captures all
information needed to reconstruct any optimization model:

1\. Sets – named collections of entities (e.g., Plants, Products,
Periods)

2\. Parameters – indexed numerical quantities, with references to CSV
files (indicating where to read the parameter data)

3\. Variables – decision variable types, domains, bounds, and index
structure

4\. Objective – a symbolic expression tree over variables and parameters

5\. Constraints – named symbolic expressions with domains and senses

IR generation is optional and governed by a user-specified configuration
parameter. When enabled, a LLM is invoked to produce the IR. Due to the
inherently non-deterministic nature of LLMs, the generation process is
constrained by a set of predefined rules embedded within the prompt to
prevent hallucinations. After generation, the IR is passed to a
validator to ensure correctness. The validator is designed to detect
common failure modes associated with LLM-generated IR. If validation
fails, the identified errors are fed back to the agent, which then
regenerates the IR.

Compilation from IR to solver code is a fully deterministic process
enabled by an IR compiler, with zero LLM calls. This means that once an
IR has been validated, it can be recompiled to any supported backend at
any time without incurring API costs or non-determinism.

The existence of the IR enables a lightweight IR compilation pipeline in
which a pre-built ir.json file together with CSV files can be compiled
and solved with zero LLM calls, see Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.5 Intermediate Representation (IR) ‣ 3 System Architecture ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
This pipeline is useful for CI/CD validation and solver regression
testing and also crucial to what-if analyses that business users usually
perform to support decision making in practice. A more detailed
discussion about the role of IR in what-if analysis can be found in
Section
[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 What-if Analysis via IR Manipulation ‣ 5 Conclusions and Discussions ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").

![Refer to caption](2605.02728v1/ir_compiler_pipeline.png)

Figure 2: IR compilation pipeline. Blue indicates an LLM-involved step,
while orange indicates a deterministic step.

### 3.6 Reporter Agent

After a successful solve, a reporter agent generates a plain-English
summary of the solution: the optimal objective value, the values of key
decision variables, and a brief interpretation of key findings and
operational suggestions in the domain language of the original problem.
This output is intended for consumption by the business user who
initiated the problem description, not by an OR expert. Refer to Section
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Solution Report Produced by Reporter Agent for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"),
[I](#A9 "Appendix I Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
and
[N](#A14 "Appendix N Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
for real examples of optimization reports produced by the reporter
agent.

### 4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP)

Consider a multi-period and multi-product supply chain network
optimization problem defined over the following sets: $`I`$ – set of
production sites (PS), $`J`$ – set of distribution centers (DC), $`K`$ –
set of customers, $`P`$ – set of products, and $`T`$ – set of periods.
Not all $`(i,j)`$ and $`(j,k)`$ pairs are connected. The network
topology is defined by a sparse set of links $`E_{IJ}\in I\times J`$ and
$`E_{JK}\in J\times K`$. The decision variables are: $`x_{ipt}`$ – units
of product $`p`$ produced at PS $`i`$ in period $`t`$, $`f_{ijpt}`$ –
units of product $`p`$ shipped from PS $`i`$ to DC $`j`$ in period $`t`$
defined only for $`(i,j)\in E_{IJ}`$, $`f_{jkpt}`$ – units of product
$`p`$ shipped from DC $`j`$ to customer $`k`$ in period $`t`$ defined
only for $`(j,k)\in E_{JK}`$, $`u_{ipt}`$ – end-of-period inventory of
product $`p`$ at PS $`i`$ in period $`t`$, $`u_{jpt}`$ – end-of-period
inventory of product $`p`$ at DC $`j`$ in period $`t`$. All variables
are continuous and non-negative and initial inventory is zero at all
facilities (PSs and DCs). The objective is to maximize annual profit:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
{maximize}\sum_{j,k,p,t}r_{p}*f_{jkpt}-\sum_{i,p,t}c^{p}_{ip}*x_{ipt}-\sum_{i,j,p,t}c^{t}_{ij}*f_{ijpt}-\sum_{j,k,p,t}c^{t}_{jk}*f_{jkpt}-\sum_{i,p,t}c^{h}_{ip}*u_{ipt}-\sum_{j,p,t}c^{h}_{jp}*u_{jpt},
``` |  |

where $`r_{p}`$ is the revenue of product $`p`$, $`c^{p}_{ip}`$ is the
cost for producing one unit of product $`p`$ at PS $`i`$, $`c^{t}_{ij}`$
is the transportation cost for shipping one unit of any product from PS
$`i`$ to DC $`j`$, $`c^{t}_{jk}`$ is the transportation cost for
shipping one unit of any product from DC $`j`$ to customer $`k`$,
$`c^{h}_{ip}`$ is the inventory holding cost for one unit of product
$`p`$ at PS $`i`$ and $`c^{h}_{jp}`$ is the inventory holding cost for
one unit of product $`p`$ at DC $`j`$. The problem is subject to the
following constraints:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle production\ \ capacity:\ \ \ \sum_{p}x_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle cap_{it}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle flow\ \ balance\ \ at\ \ production\ \ sites:\ \ \ u_{ip,t-1}+x_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{j}f_{ijpt}+u_{ipt}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,p\in P,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle inventory\ \ limit\ \ at\ \ production\ \ sites:\ \ \ \sum_{p}u_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle lim_{i}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle flow\ \ balance\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ u_{jp,t-1}+\sum_{i}f_{ijpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{k}f_{jkpt}+u_{jpt}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,p\in P,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle throughput\ \ capacity\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ \sum_{p,k}f_{jkpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle cap_{jt}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle inventory\ \ limit\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ \sum_{p}u_{jpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle lim_{j}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle demand\ \ requirements:\ \ \ \sum_{j}f_{jkpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle dem_{kpt}\ \ \ \ \forall k\in K,p\in P,t\in T,`$ |  |

where $`cap_{it}`$ is the production capacity at PS $`i`$ in period
$`t`$, $`cap_{jt}`$ is the throughput capacity at DC $`j`$ in period
$`t`$, $`limit_{i}`$ is the inventory limit at production site $`i`$,
$`limit_{j}`$ is the inventory limit at distribution center $`j`$, and
$`dem_{kpt}`$ is the demand of customer $`k`$ for product $`p`$ in
period $`t`$.

To prepare the data for this problem instance, all numerical data were
generated synthetically with a fixed random seed 42 to ensure
reproducibility. The problem instance comprises 50 PSs, 50 DCs, 500
customers, 500 products, and 12 monthly planning periods. All facilities
and customers are placed on a $`1000\times 1000`$ unit grid. PSs are
drawn uniformly from the interior band $`[200,800]^{2}`$, DCs from the
near-full grid $`[50,950]^{2}`$, and customers are sampled from 20
Gaussian clusters whose centers are drawn uniformly from
$`[100,900]^{2}`$, with per-cluster standard deviation $`\sigma=30`$
units. Each PS is connected to its 8 nearest DCs by a directed link,
yielding a sparse PS$`\to`$DC subnetwork; isolated DCs (those with no
incoming link) are connected to their single nearest PS as a fallback,
resulting in 404 PS$`\to`$DC links in total. Similarly, each DC is
connected to its 20 nearest customers for the DC$`\to`$customer links;
any customer left uncovered is connected to its nearest DC, giving 1,065
DC$`\to`$customer links in total. Transportation costs are proportional
to Euclidean distance (\$0.05 per product unit per distance unit on the
PS$`\to`$DC leg and \$0.08 per product unit per distance unit on the
DC$`\to`$customer leg) with independent multiplicative noise that
follows a distribution $`U(0.9,1.1)`$. Unit revenues are drawn from a
log-normal distribution with parameters $`\mu=3.9`$ and $`\sigma=0.6`$,
giving a median price of approximately \$49, a mean of approximately
\$59, and a coefficient of variation of 0.66. Production costs for each
(PS, product) pair are set to a site-level efficiency factor drawn from
distribution $`U(0.30,0.55)`$ multiplied by the product revenue,
multiplied by independent noise that follows distribution
$`U(0.85,1.15)`$. Inventory holding costs are set to $`U(1.0\%,2.0\%)`$
of product revenue per period at PSs and $`U(0.8\%,1.8\%)`$ at DCs.
Capacities are set after demand data to make sure the problem instance
is feasible. For each DC $`j`$, the throughput capacity is set to
$`1.5D_{jt}`$ (with $`\pm 5\%`$ multiplicative noise), where $`D_{jt}`$
is the total demand of all customers that are reachable by DC $`j`$ in
period $`t`$. For each production site $`i`$, the production capacity is
set to $`1.5D_{it}`$ (with $`\pm 5\%`$ multiplicative noise), where
$`D_{it}`$ is the total demand of all customers that are reachable by PS
$`i`$ in period $`t`$. This allocation ensures that the aggregate
production capacity across all sites is at least $`1.5\times`$ total
system demand in every period, while each site individually covers its
mandatory supply obligations. A floor of 10,000 units is applied to all
capacity parameters. Storage capacities at PSs are drawn from
distribution $`U(5{,}000,12{,}000)`$ and at DCs from distribution
$`U(8{,}000,15{,}000)`$. The resulting system-wide production-to-demand
ratio ranges from 1.52 in December (the peak demand month) to 2.49, with
a period-average of approximately 1.98. Each customer is assigned a
random subset of 40–80 products (drawn uniformly without replacement
from the full product set). Per-product base demand for each customer is
drawn from a log-normal distribution with $`\mu=2.5`$ and
$`\sigma=0.6`$, and scaled by a monthly seasonal multiplier that follows
the pattern
$`s_{t}\in\{0.85,0.80,0.90,1.00,1.05,1.10,1.15,1.10,1.05,1.00,0.95,1.30\}`$
for months $`t=1,\ldots,12`$, peaking in December ($`+30\%`$). An
independent uniform noise factor that follows distribution
$`U(0.8,1.2)`$ is applied to each (customer, product, period) triple,
and entries that round to zero are dropped. The resulting demand table
contains 361,092 non-zero entries across 500 customers, 500 products,
and 12 periods. The resulting number of variables and number of
constraints are summarized in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
This is a large-scale pure LP problem with 9,714,000 variables and
963,492 constraints.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Number of Variables |  |  |  | Number of Constraints |  |  |
|  | production | shipment | inventory |  | inventory balance | demand | capacity |
| Individual | 300,000 | 8,814,000 | 600,000 |  |    600,000 | 361,092 | 2,400 |
| Total |  | 9,714,000 |  |  |  | 963,492 |  |

Table 1: Number of variables and number of constraints

ORPilot was then tested on this problem instance. In consideration of
both cost and speed, I selected Deepseek-Chat model as the LLM for this
experiment. Considering the scale of this problem, Gurobi was selected
as the optimization solver. The purpose of this experiment is to test
the performance of each component in the ORPilot standard pipeline in
Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 System Architecture ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
The test results for each component are presented in the following
paragraphs in sequence.

1.  1.
    Interview Agent. A standard ORPilot pipeline starts with a
    conversation with the interview agent. The whole conversation with
    the interview agent obtained from this experiment is presented in
    Section
    [A](#A1 "Appendix A Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    We see that the interview agent was able to guide the user to
    describe the problem thoroughly and ask important clarifying
    questions like “does this model handle a single product or multiple
    products" to fully grasp every detail of the model. When the agent
    thought it had all the necessary information to formulate the model,
    it provided a summary of the problem and asked the user to confirm
    whether any important details was not captured. This offered the
    user an opportunity to correct problem specifications if needed. For
    example, the interview agent automatically assumed that the
    inventory storage capacity, production cost, inventory holding cost
    and revenue were time-dependent parameters and there were initial
    inventories at production sites and distribution centers. However,
    later the user added a clarification that the inventory storage
    capacity, production cost, inventory holding cost and revenue did
    not vary across time, and that there were no initial inventories.
    Then the agent was able to correct the problem specifications
    accordingly by removing the time index from these parameters and
    making initial inventory parameter optional.
2.  2.
    Data Collection Agent and Parameter Computation Agent. After the
    interview is finished, the standard pipeline calls the data
    collection agent and parameter computation agent to prepare the data
    needed for modeling this problem. The data collection agent
    instructs the user on what CSV files are needed and what are the
    corresponding schema through an interactive conversation, and then
    the data computation agent decides if any parameters need to be
    computed based on the raw data the user provided. The conversation
    between the data collection agent and the user is presented in
    Section
    [B](#A2 "Appendix B Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    We see that the agent clearly listed out all the 12 CSV files
    required for modeling this problem along with the associated schema.
    Once the user provided the required CSV files, the parameter
    computation agent then worked on the files and decided no additional
    CSV file was needed for modeling the problem.
3.  3.
    Code Generation Agent. Once parameter computation is finished,
    ORPilot reads the generated CSV files and serializes them into a
    JSON object named “data". Then the code generation agent generates
    the solver code based on the problem specifications and the JSON
    object. The generated solver code is presented in Section
    [C](#A3 "Appendix C Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
4.  4.
    Code Execution. ORPilot executes the generated solver code in a
    sandbox, parses the optimization results and produces the output CSV
    files. Specifically, in this problem, the code was executed
    successfully without any error, and 5 output CSV files containing
    the values of the decision variables were produced. The details of
    these 5 output CSV files can be found in Section
    [D](#A4 "Appendix D Solution Report Produced by Reporter Agent for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
5.  5.
    Reporter Agent. Once the optimization model is solved successfully,
    the reporter agent looks at the output CSV files and produces a
    report that explains what each output CSV file contains and main
    findings in the solution. The report generated for this problem is
    presented in Section
    [D](#A4 "Appendix D Solution Report Produced by Reporter Agent for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
6.  6.
    IR generation. The generated IR for this problem is presented in
    Section
    [E](#A5 "Appendix E Generated IR for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    The correctness of the IR was tested by recompiling it to solver
    code and executed with the same data in a secured sandbox
    environment. The process returned the same solution as that from the
    code execution step of the original run.

### 4.2 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization with Binary Decisions (MIP)

Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
shows that ORPilot is able to tackle a pure LP problem with real-life
sized data. In this experiment, I further escalated this problem by
introducing binary decision variables to make it a MIP problem and
evaluated the performance of ORPilot.

The binary decisions added to this problem are the opening decisions of
PSs and DCs. In any period, the user is allowed to open a PS or a DC
with a fixed opening cost incurred. Once a PS or a DC is opened, it
remains open for the rest of the periods. For any period in which a PS
or DC is open, a fixed operating cost will be incurred. The fixed
opening cost and operating cost numbers are generated as random draws
calibrated to be economically meaningful relative to the revenue and
flow volumes in the problem instance. To make the problem solvable in a
reasonable amount of time, 25 PSs (out of 50), 25 DCs (out of 50) and
250 customers (out of 500) were retained from the original LP problem,
while all 500 products and 12 monthly periods were kept unchanged. The
transportation links were subsetted accordingly, reducing PS$`\to`$DC
links from 404 to 109 and DC$`\to`$customer links from 1,065 to 299.

The objective of this MIP problem can be given as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{maximize}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{j,k,p,t}r_{p}*f_{jkpt}-\sum_{i,p,t}c^{p}_{ip}*x_{ipt}-\sum_{i,j,p,t}c^{t}_{ij}*f_{ijpt}-\sum_{j,k,p,t}c^{t}_{jk}*f_{jkpt}-\sum_{i,p,t}c^{h}_{ip}*u_{ipt}-\sum_{j,p,t}c^{h}_{jp}*u_{jpt}`$ |  |
|  |  |  | $`\displaystyle-\sum_{i}c^{o}_{i}*o_{i,t=12}-\sum_{j}c^{o}_{j}*o_{j,t=12}-\sum_{i,t}c^{op}_{i}*o_{it}-\sum_{j,t}c^{op}_{j}*o_{jt},`$ |  |

where $`c^{o}_{i}`$ is the fixed opening cost of PS $`i`$, $`c^{o}_{j}`$
is the fixed opening cost of DC $`j`$, $`c^{op}_{i}`$ is the fixed
operating cost of PS $`i`$, and $`c^{op}_{j}`$ is the fixed operating
cost of DC $`j`$, $`o_{it}`$ and $`o_{jt}`$ are binary decision
variables denoting whether PS $`i`$ and DC $`j`$ are open in period
$`t`$. One trick to calculate the fixed opening cost for a PS or DC is
to multiply the opening cost with $`o_{it}`$ or $`o_{jt}`$ in the last
period, due to the assumption that once a facility is open it remains
open for the rest of the periods. This problem is subject to the
following constraints:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle production\ \ capacity:\ \ \ \sum_{p}x_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle cap_{it}*o_{it}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle flow\ \ balance\ \ at\ \ production\ \ sites:\ \ \ u_{ip,t-1}+x_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{j}f_{ijpt}+u_{ipt}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,p\in P,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle inventory\ \ limit\ \ at\ \ production\ \ sites:\ \ \ \sum_{p}u_{ipt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle lim_{i}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle flow\ \ balance\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ u_{jp,t-1}+\sum_{i}f_{ijpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{k}f_{jkpt}+u_{jpt}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,p\in P,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle throughput\ \ capacity\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ \sum_{p,k}f_{jkpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle cap_{jt}*o_{jt}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle inventory\ \ limit\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\ \ \ \sum_{p}u_{jpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle lim_{j}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle demand\ \ requirements:\ \ \ \sum_{j}f_{jkpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle dem_{kpt}\ \ \ \ \forall k\in K,p\in P,t\in T`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle production\ \ site\ \ opening\ \ logic:\ \ \ o_{it}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq`$ | $`\displaystyle o_{i,t-1}\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,t=2,3,...,12`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle distribution\ \ center\ \ opening\ \ logic:\ \ \ o_{jt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq`$ | $`\displaystyle o_{j,t-1}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t=2,3,...,12`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle linking\ \ inflows\ \ to\ \ open\ \ status\ \ at\ \ distribution\ \ centers:\sum_{p,i}f_{ijpt}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle(cap_{jt}+lim_{j})*o_{jt}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J,t\in T.`$ |  |

This formulation results in 2,898,000 continuous variables, 600 binary
variables, and 2,102,050 constraints.

ORPilot was then tested on this problem instance. As the problem was
escalated to a MIP model, I selected a more capable LLM,
Deepseek-Reasoner model for this experiment. Gurobi was selected as the
optimization solver. The test results for each component are presented
in the following paragraphs in sequence.

1.  1.
    Interview Agent. The whole conversation with the interview agent
    obtained from this experiment is presented in Section
    [F](#A6 "Appendix F Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    The conversation is similar to that in Section
    [A](#A1 "Appendix A Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    Regarding the newly added facility opening decisions, the agent was
    able to ask questions to clarify the facility opening rules.
2.  2.
    Data Collection Agent and Parameter Computation Agent. The
    conversation between the data collection agent and the user is shown
    in Section
    [G](#A7 "Appendix G Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    The data collection agent specified 18 CSV files needed for this
    problem with their corresponding schema and the parameter
    computation agent calculated a BigM value to be used in constraints
    linking continuous variables to binary variables.
3.  3.
    Code Generation Agent. The generated solver code is given in
    Appendix
    [H](#A8 "Appendix H Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    An interesting finding is that from the comments the LLM wrote, it
    realized the trick of calculating the total fixed opening cost by
    multiplying the opening cost with $`o_{it}`$ or $`o_{jt}`$ in the
    last period, however, it still decided to adopt a more explicit
    approach by adding up $`c^{o}_{i}*(o_{i,t}-o_{i,t-1})`$ and
    $`c^{o}_{j}*(o_{j,t}-o_{j,t-1})`$ across all periods except for the
    first period, which is also correct.
4.  4.
    Code Execution. In this problem, the code was executed successfully
    without any error, and 7 output CSV files containing the values of
    the decision variables were produced. The details of these 7 output
    CSV files can be found in Section
    [I](#A9 "Appendix I Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
5.  5.
    Reporter Agent. The report generated for this problem is presented
    in Section
    [I](#A9 "Appendix I Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
6.  6.
    IR generation. The IR generated for this problem is presented in
    Section
    [J](#A10 "Appendix J Generated IR for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    The correctness of the IR was tested by recompiling it to solver
    code and executed with the same data in a secured sandbox
    environment. The process returned the same solution as that from the
    code execution step of the original run.

### 4.3 Large-Scale Freight Assignment Problem (Pure IP)

Consider a freight assignment problem, where the user has a set of
shipments $`I`$ to assign to a set of carriers $`J`$. Each shipment has
its own revenue $`r_{i}`$, and the assignment cost for assigning
shipment $`i`$ to carrier $`j`$ is $`c_{ij}`$. The decision variables
are $`x_{ij}`$, which are binary variables representing whether shipment
$`i`$ is assigned to carrier $`j`$. Any shipment can be left unassigned
and there is no penalty for not assigning a shipment. The objective of
is to maximize the profit for assigning the shipments:

|     |                                          |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       {maximize}\sum_{ij}(r_{i}-c_{ij})x_{ij}.
       ```                                       |     |

This problem is subject to the following constraints:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle carrier\ \ capacity:\ \ \ \sum_{i}o_{ij}x_{ij}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle cap_{j}\ \ \ \ \forall j\in J`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle each\ \ shipment\ \ assigned\ \ at\ \ most\ \ once:\ \ \ \sum_{j}x_{ij}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle 1\ \ \ \ \forall i\in I,`$ |  |

where $`o_{ij}`$ is the capacity the shipment $`i`$ occupies on carrier
$`j`$ if shipment $`i`$ is assigned to carrier $`j`$ and $`cap_{j}`$ is
the capacity of carrier $`j`$.

All data are generated synthetically with a fixed random seed 42 to
ensure reproducibility. The instance comprises 400 carriers and 3,200
shipments, yielding a pure IP problem with 1,280,000 binary decision
variables. Each carrier is assigned a fixed depot location drawn
uniformly from a 1,000 × 1,000 unit grid. Each shipment has an origin
point, also drawn uniformly from the same grid. Each carrier has a
per-unit-distance cost rate drawn from distribution $`U(0.04,0.12)`$ and
a handling efficiency factor drawn from distribution $`U(0.85,1.15)`$.
Carrier weight capacities are set after shipment weights are generated:
the target per-carrier capacity is
$`1.3\times(\text{total demand}/\text{number of carriers})`$, and
individual capacities are drawn from distribution $`U(0.7,1.3)`$ times
that target, giving a fleet-wide capacity-to-demand ratio of 1.31 and a
per-carrier range of 670 –1,240 kg. Shipment weights are drawn from a
log-normal distribution with parameters $`\mu=4.4`$ and $`\sigma=0.5`$
(median $`\approx`$ 81 kg), truncated at a minimum of 5 kg. Unit revenue
for each shipment is its weight multiplied by a price factor drawn from
distribution $`U(2.5,6.0)`$, yielding revenues between \$57 and \$2,181.
For each shipment-carrier pair $`(i,j)`$, the assignment cost is
computed as cost
$`\text{rate}_{j}\times w_{i}\times d_{ij}/100+\epsilon_{ij}`$, where
$`w_{i}`$ is the weight of shipment $`i`$, $`d_{ij}`$ is the Euclidean
distance from carrier $`j`$’s depot to shipment $`i`$’s origin and
$`\epsilon_{ij}\sim U(20,80)`$ is a handling fee. The capacity consumed
when carrier $`j`$ takes shipment $`i`$ is
$`r_{ij}=w_{i}\times h_{j}\times\eta_{ij}`$, where
$`h_{j}\sim U(0.85,1.15)`$ is the carrier’s loading efficiency and
$`\eta_{ij}\sim U(0.92,1.08)`$ is a per-pair noise term. This
carrier-specific resource consumption is what distinguishes the instance
as a generalized assignment problem rather than a standard bin-packing
formulation.

ORPilot was then tested on this problem instance with Deepseek-Chat as
the LLM and Gurobi as the optimization solver. The test results for each
component are presented in the following paragraphs in sequence.

1.  1.
    Interview Agent. The whole conversation with the interview agent
    obtained from this experiment is presented in Section
    [K](#A11 "Appendix K Conversation History between Interview Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    This is a conceptually easier model to formulate than the problems
    in Section
    [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
    and
    [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization with Binary Decisions (MIP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"),
    hence the agent needed fewer rounds of conversations to confirm the
    problem specifications.
2.  2.
    Data Collection Agent and Parameter Computation Agent. The
    conversation between the data collection agent and the user is shown
    in Section
    [L](#A12 "Appendix L Conversation History between Data Collection Agent and User for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    The data collection agent specified 5 CSV files needed for this
    problem with their corresponding schema. The parameter computation
    agent didn’t compute any additional parameters for this problem.
3.  3.
    Code Generation Agent. The generated solver code is given in Section
    [M](#A13 "Appendix M Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
4.  4.
    Code Execution. In this problem, the code was executed successfully
    without any error, and only one output CSV file containing the
    values of the decision variables was produced. The details of the
    produced output CSV file can be found in Section
    [N](#A14 "Appendix N Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
5.  5.
    Reporter Agent. The report generated for this problem is presented
    in Section
    [N](#A14 "Appendix N Solution Report for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
6.  6.
    The generated IR for this problem is presented in Section
    [O](#A15 "Appendix O Generated IR for Problem in Section ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
    A recompilation of the IR with the same data showed exactly the same
    solution.

### 4.4 Academic Benchmarks

Existing LLM-for-OR tools and ORPilot are targeted at different types of
problems. While most existing tools strive to improve the accuracy on
solving textbook style OR problems (unambiguous problem descriptions in
one go and clean model-ready data), ORPilot is aimed at more industrial
style real-life OR problems with large scale data. However, in order to
compare ORPilot with other tools, I evaluated the accuracy performance
of ORPilot on three academic benchmarks: IndustryOR, NL4OPT and NLP4LP,
which existing tools are usually evaluated on, although these three
benchmarks are not quite in the comfort zone of ORPilot.

Since ORPilot is originally designed for dialog-based problem
description intake, not for prepared problem text, the standard pipeline
of ORPilot cannot be directly applied to the academic benchmarks. Hence,
I designed a benchmark mode for the ORPilot pipeline specially for
running benchmark tests.

IndustryOR \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] is a benchmark of 100 real-world
industrial OR problems drawn from supply chain, scheduling, routing, and
resource allocation. Problems are labeled as easy (39 instances), medium
(41 instances), or hard (20 instances). It is the most industrially
representative of the three benchmarks evaluated here. NL4OPT
\[[5](#bib.bib5)\] is an academic benchmark of natural-language linear
programming problems, originally introduced as a shared task at NeurIPS
2022. Each problem is a self-contained textbook-style LP with numerical
data embedded in the problem text. I evaluated on the test split and
restricted to problems that have a finite optimal solution (skipping
infeasible or unbounded instances). NLP4LP \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\] is a gated benchmark (udell-lab/NLP4LP)
containing a diverse set of LP problems with natural-language
descriptions and associated parameter tables. It is more challenging
than NL4OPT in that the problems are longer, more ambiguously stated,
and include parameter data as structured JSON rather than inline text.

For the existing LLM-for-OR tools to compare, I selected three
representative works to compare: LLMOPT \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], ORLM
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\] and OptiMUS \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2),
[3](#bib.bib3)\] due to their similar pipeline to ORPilot. The test
results are summarized in Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Academic Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
All test results of ORPilot were obtained using the pulp solver backend.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | IndustryOR |  |  | NL4OPT |  |  | NLP4LP |  |
|  | SA | AST |  | SA | AST |  | SA | AST |
| LLMOPT with Qwen1.5-14B | 46.0% | 8.35s |  | 93.0% | 3.07s |  | 83.8% | 7.00s |
| ORLM with LLaMa3-8B | 38.0% |    - |  | 85.7% |    - |  |    - |    - |
| ORLM with Deepseek-Math | 33.0% |    - |  | 86.5% |    - |  | 72.9% |    - |
| OptiMUS0.3 with GPT-4o | 37.0% |    - |  | 86.6% |    - |  | 73.7% |    - |
| OptiMUS0.3 with o1 | 46.0% |    - |  |    - |    - |  | 80.6% |    - |
| ORPilot with Claude Snonnet 4.6 | 75.0% | 31.0s |  | 73.2% | 16.3s |  | 79.8% | 14.8s |
````
