Table 2: Comparison between ORPilot and existing tools on solving
accuracy (SA) and average solving time (AST)

On IndustryOR benchmark, a notable observation is that ORPilot with
GPT-4o (46% overall) exceeds the 37% accuracy reported for OptiMUS-0.3
with GPT-4o \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] on this benchmark, when using the same
underlying LLM. Note that GPT-4o is no longer among the top models by
2026. The reason why GPT-4o was selected to be tested with ORPilot is to
ensure ORPilot was using the same LLM as OptMUS0.3 for a fair
comparison. Another observation is that ORPilot with the most advanced
commercial LLMs as of 2026 significantly outperforms other tools with
models fine-tuned on similar tasks in terms of accuracy, with
DeepSeek-Reasoner achieving an accuracy (74%) comparable to
Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (75%) but at substantially higher latency. For
latency-sensitive applications, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 is the preferred LLM.
However, for cost sensitive applications, Deepseek-Reasoner is
undoubtedly the top choice. Overall, it can be concluded that ORPilot
achieves a better accuracy performance as compared to other tools, due
to the more industrial nature of IndustryOR dataset.

On NL4OPT and NLP4LP datasets, however, ORPilot is showing an inferior
accuracy performance, as these problems are less industrial in nature.

## 5 Conclusions and Discussions

This paper presents ORPilot, a production-oriented LLM-powered AI agent
for OR modeling with a design principle that mirrors how OR consultants
would work with business users for modeling their problems. By
introducing four novel pipeline components – a conversational interview
agent, a data collection agent, a parameter computation agent, and a
solver-agnostic Intermediate Representation (IR), ORPilot addresses the
full gap between an unconstrained business dialog and a deployable and
reproducible optimization model. These components have no counterpart in
most existing LLM-for-OR tools, which operate exclusively in the
idealized setting of clean, complete and inline problem descriptions.

Experimental results in Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")
show that ORPilot works well with OR problems with large scale data in
supply chain industry and delivers a superior performance than existing
LLM-for-OR tools when evaluated on industry-style academic benchmark
problems. I believe that the pipeline introduced here – iterative
problem elicitation, data collection, automated parameter derivation,
and IR-based reproducibility, represents a necessary and general
framework for any serious LLM-for-OR production-level deployment, and I
hope it will serve as a foundation for future work in this area.
Although the experimental results establish ORPilot as a competitive
production-grade pipeline prototype, but they also expose a few
structural limitations that define the most productive directions for
future work.

### 5.1 Optimal Solution Validation

The current pipeline of ORPilot does not have any mechanism to examine
the solution when an optimal solution is produced. The retry loop is
only triggered when the model generated runs into an error,
infeasibility or unboundedness. However, the generated model can be
semantically wrong (misidentifying a decision variable, omitting a
constraint, or misinterpreting a bound) yet still produces an optimal
solution. In fact, on the three academic benchmarks (IndustryOR, NL4OPT
and NLP4LP), most of the failed cases of ORPilot are due to a wrong
optimal objective value without entering any retry loop.

Addressing this limitation requires a solution validation layer between
the solver and the reporter. A solution validation agent prompted with
the original problem description and the full solution vector could
verify that the reported values satisfy the business constraints as
stated in natural language, that variable assignments are semantically
meaningful, and that the solution is not merely optimal within a
misspecified model. When this agent decides the optimal solution is
semantically wrong, it triggers the retry loop to regenerate the model
with the new message the solution validation agent produces. This is
analogous to the backward-reflection step proposed in Chain-of-Experts
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\], but applied to the solution rather than to the
formulation. The pipeline with a solution validation agent can be
illustrated by the diagram in Figure
[3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Optimal Solution Validation ‣ 5 Conclusions and Discussions ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").

![Refer to caption](2605.02728v1/solution_validation_pipeline.png)

Figure 3: ORPilot pipeline with a solution validation agent. Blue
indicates an LLM-involved step, while orange indicates a deterministic
step. Double arrows in opposite directions indicate the interactive
nature of this step. Solid arrows represent unconditional transitions
between steps, while dashed arrows represent conditional transitions
between steps.

However, adding another LLM-powered agent to examine the semantical
correctness of the optimal solution of the generated model is a
double-edged sword. While it could identify possible optimal solutions
that are semantically wrong, it could also produce false positives
(flagging solutions that are semantically correct as wrong and
triggering the retry loop), which could turn a correct solution into a
wrong solution in the end. Some preliminary experiments I conducted have
shown that such an agent would bring more issues than benefits without a
fine-tuned prompt or heuristic. Developing robust prompts or heuristics
for validating optimal solutions generated by LLM-for-OR tools is an
important open problem for the field, not only for ORPilot.

### 5.2 Infeasibility and Unboundedness Analysis

A semantically wrong model generated by LLM-for-OR tools could produce
an optimal solution. Conversely, a semantically correct model could run
into infeasibility/unboundedness due to the nature of the data provided
or the constraints specified (e.g., the total capacity of all facilities
is not large enough to satisfy the demands of all customers in a supply
chain problem). ORPilot’s retry loop treats infeasibility/unboundedness
as a recoverable failure: when the solver returns an infeasible signal,
the error is fed back to the LLM with a prompt to revise the model, and
a new attempt is made. This heuristic is effective when
infeasibility/unboundedness is caused by a modeling error (e.g., a
misspecified constraint, an incorrect bound, or a missing relaxation).
However, it is counterproductive when infeasibility is inherent to the
problem as specified. No reformulation of the model will yield a
feasible solution because the user’s constraints are mutually
contradictory or the problem data make the feasible region empty. In
this case, the retry loop wastes API calls and latency and ultimately
fails after exhausting its budget, reporting a failure that could have
been diagnosed immediately.

Two complementary capabilities are needed. First, an infeasibility
classifier should distinguish between (1) formulation infeasibility –
the model as written is infeasible due to a modeling error, for which a
retry is appropriate and (2) problem infeasibility – the constraints
implied by the problem description are inherently contradictory, for
which the correct response is to inform the user and terminate. A
lightweight classifier trained on solver status codes, constraint
structure, and LLM-extracted semantic features could make this
distinction before invoking the retry loop. Second, for confirmed
problem infeasibility, an infeasibility diagnosis agent should apply
techniques from the OR literature, e.g., irreducible infeasible
subsystems (IIS) extraction or constraint relaxation enumeration, to
identify the minimal conflicting subset of constraints and translate it
back into natural-language terms the user can understand. This closes
the loop for business users: rather than a generic failure message, they
receive an explanation such as “the weekly production capacity
constraint conflicts with the minimum demand requirement in week 3 and
one of these must be relaxed." Such explanations are standard output
from commercial solver tools (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX) but are not yet
integrated into any LLM-for-OR tools.

### 5.3 Fine-Tuned Language Models for OR Modeling

All ORPilot results reported in this paper are based on general-purpose
frontier LLMs (e.g., Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-Reasoner) via API. This
approach has significant advantages – no training infrastructure,
immediate access to the latest models, but also significant drawbacks –
API cost, latency, data privacy constraints, and a hard dependency on
external services for a production system.

The IR structure in ORPilot provides a natural training signal for
fine-tuning. Each successful ORPilot run produces a (problem
specification, ir.json) pair that is a high-quality supervised training
example. The input is an unambiguous natural-language problem
description with the schema information of associated data tables needed
for building the OR model and the output is a structurally valid,
solver-verified IR that compiles correctly to executable code. Unlike
raw solver code, which is backend-specific, verbose, and sensitive to
API idiom, the IR is compact, backend-agnostic, and schema-validated,
making it a substantially cleaner training target. In practice, a
smaller open-weights LLM (e.g., a 7B or 13B parameter model) can be
trained to generate IR JSON from problem specifications, using
successful and verified ORPilot runs as supervised examples.

The current pipeline of ORPilot uses IR generation as a post-processing
step after an optimal solution is generated, see Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 System Architecture ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
IR generation was not designed as a step prior to solver code generation
in ORPilot in the first place. This is because the experiments I
conducted showed LLM-powered IR generation was not very robust and
stable using only problem specifications and data table schemas. Feeding
artifacts like solver code (model.py) together into LLMs can enhance the
quality of the generated IR.

However, with fine-tuned LLMs that use verified IRs as the learning
target, a new pipeline can be established which employs IR generation
prior to solver code generation, see Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Fine-Tuned Language Models for OR Modeling ‣ 5 Conclusions and Discussions ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").
As the fine-tuning process is expected to significantly improve the
quality of the generated IR, IR generation can serve as a stable
component that would not impact the accuracy of the downstream steps.
Since ORPilot has a deterministic IR compiler, solver code generation in
this new pipeline will be a deterministic step. This decouples the
modeling intelligence (LLM to IR) from the compilation step (IR to
solver code), concentrating the LLM’s task on structured JSON generation
rather than solver API syntax.

![Refer to caption](2605.02728v1/ir_in_the_middle_pipeline.png)

Figure 4: ORPilot pipeline with IR generation prior to generating solver
code. Blue indicates an LLM-involved step, while orange indicates a
deterministic step. Double arrows in opposite directions indicate the
interactive nature of this step. Solid arrows represent unconditional
transitions between steps, while dashed arrows represent conditional
transitions between steps.

This direction is consistent with work on LLM fine-tuning for OR,
including ORLM \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] and LLaMoCo \[[11](#bib.bib11)\], but
benefits from the IR’s cleaner target structure and the availability of
verified training data generated by the ORPilot pipeline itself.

### 5.4 What-if Analysis via IR Manipulation

A natural extension of the IR’s reproducibility and portability
properties is systematic what-if analysis. Once a model has been solved
and its IR persists as a validated JSON artifact, a business user may
wish to explore how the optimal solution changes under modified
assumptions without re-engaging the LLM or re-specifying the problem
from scratch.

What-if queries fall into two structurally distinct categories, and the
IR structure is able to support both. The first category is data changes
– modifications to parameter values that leave the model structure
intact. Examples include asking “what if demand increases by 20% in Q3?"
or “what if the cost of raw material B rises to \$15 per unit?" In these
cases, only the CSV files referenced by the IR need to be updated and
the IR JSON itself is unchanged. The deterministic compiler then
recompiles the same IR against the new data and a re-solve is triggered,
which is a zero-LLM-call operation. This form of sensitivity analysis is
already latent in the current architecture and requires only a thin
user-facing interface to expose it.

The second category is structural changes: modifications to constraints,
objectives or variable domains that alter the model’s mathematical form.
Examples include “what if we add a constraint that no single supplier
accounts for more than 40% of total procurement?" or “what if we remove
the overtime limit and instead penalize it in the objective?" These
changes require editing the IR – adding, removing, or modifying
constraint or objective terms. Because the IR is a typed,
schema-validated document with a well-defined expression tree, such
edits are localized and predictable: adding a constraint is a matter of
appending a new constraint object with the appropriate domain and
expression, rather than modifying dozens of lines of solver-specific
code.

A what-if analysis agent can be added into the current IR compilation
pipeline (see Figure
[5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.4 What-if Analysis via IR Manipulation ‣ 5 Conclusions and Discussions ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling"))
which accepts natural-language change requests, classifies them as data
changes or structural changes, and either updates the relevant values in
CSV files or generate a targeted IR modification. The LLM’s task in this
setting is substantially simpler than full model generation: it operates
on a verified IR and only needs to express an incremental change in the
same structured schema. This narrower task is well-suited to a
fine-tuned or smaller LLM as discussed in Section
[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Fine-Tuned Language Models for OR Modeling ‣ 5 Conclusions and Discussions ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling").

![Refer to caption](2605.02728v1/what_if_pipeline.png)

Figure 5: ORPilot pipeline with a what-if analysis agent. Blue indicates
an LLM-involved step, while orange indicates a deterministic step.

This capability would bring ORPilot significantly closer to the vision
articulated by \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] of a conversational
decision-optimization tool that supports iterative exploration of the
solution space, not being just a one-shot model builder, which is a
significant enabler for enterprise adoption.

### 5.5 Database Connection

A key limitation of the current ORPilot pipeline is its reliance on
user-prepared CSV files as the data interface. While this design keeps
the system lightweight and portable, it places a significant burden on
practitioners, who must extract, transform, and format data from their
operational systems before optimization can begin. A natural and
impactful extension of ORPilot is to eliminate this preprocessing step
through native database connectivity.

In future versions, ORPilot could accept a database connection string –
pointing to a relational database, data warehouse, or enterprise
resource planning (ERP) system and autonomously perform the data
engineering tasks currently delegated to the user. This capability would
unfold in three stages. First, a schema discovery phase would catalog
the available tables, columns, data types, foreign key relationships,
and cardinalities, producing a structured representation of what data
the system has access to. Second, a data sufficiency assessment phase
would evaluate whether the discovered schema contains the entities and
relationships required to instantiate the optimization model identified
during the interview phase. Drawing on the IR specification, ORPilot
would map each required set, parameter, and variable domain to candidate
tables in the database, flagging gaps where data is absent or ambiguous
and querying the user only for genuinely missing information rather than
demanding a complete data hand-off upfront. Third, a model-ready data
preparation phase would issue the necessary SQL queries, perform unit
validation, resolve naming inconsistencies, and materialize the result
as the structured inputs consumed by the IR compiler all transparently,
without requiring the user to write a single query.

This architecture would bring ORPilot substantially closer to the vision
of end-to-end decision support: a practitioner could describe their OR
problem in natural language, grant the system read access to their
existing database, and receive a solved, deployable optimization model
with minimal manual intervention. It would also make re-optimization
operationally practical – as the underlying database is updated with new
demand signals, cost figures, or capacity changes, the model could be
rebuilt and re-solved automatically, enabling near-real-time decision
support rather than one-off studies.

Several technical challenges merit attention in pursuing this direction.
Semantic alignment between database schemas and optimization concepts is
non-trivial; a table named orders in one organization may correspond to
demand in another, and the LLM agent responsible for schema mapping must
resolve such ambiguities reliably. Handling sparse or missing data
requires robust imputation and flagging strategies so that the resulting
model is both tractable and trustworthy. Privacy and access control are
also important considerations, as practitioners may only be able to
grant query-level access to subsets of their data; the system must
respect these boundaries while still assembling complete model inputs.
Finally, for very large databases, scalable query planning and data
sampling strategies will be necessary to keep the data preparation phase
practical within the time constraints of an interactive optimization
workflow.

### 5.6 Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) System

The current approach to improving ORPilot’s reliability follows an
empirical, rule-accumulation paradigm: when a failure mode is identified
through testing, such as a hallucinated column name, an incorrect sparse
network encoding, or a malformed IR expression, a corrective rule is
appended to the relevant system prompt. This strategy is effective in
the short term, as each new rule directly addresses an observed failure
and can be validated immediately through re-testing. However, it is
fundamentally unsustainable at scale. As the library of rules grows,
prompts become increasingly long, placing pressure on the context
windows of the underlying language models, increasing inference latency
and cost, and diluting the signal-to-noise ratio of the prompt itself. A
model attending to a prompt containing hundreds of rules may fail to
surface the specific guidance most relevant to the problem at hand.

A more principled and scalable alternative is to replace static and
monolithic prompts with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
architecture. Under this design, ORPilot would maintain a curated
knowledge base of high-quality examples, including reference IR
specifications for canonical problem classes, correct solver code for
representative model structures, and documented patterns for common
modeling challenges such as inventory balance constraints, sparse
network flows, and multi-period temporal dependencies. Rather than
embedding all of this knowledge statically in every prompt, agents would
issue a semantic query against the knowledge base before each generation
step, retrieving only the most relevant examples for the specific
problem structure currently being modeled. The retrieved examples would
be injected dynamically into the prompt context, providing targeted,
high-precision guidance without the overhead of irrelevant rules.

This architecture would yield several concrete benefits beyond prompt
length control. First, it decouples knowledge maintenance from prompt
engineering: adding a new problem type or correcting a modeling pattern
becomes an operation on the knowledge base rather than a prompt rewrite,
making the system easier to maintain and extend. Second, retrieval-based
selection is inherently adaptive, a routing problem would surface
arc-flow examples and subtour elimination patterns, while an inventory
management problem would retrieve temporal balance constraints and
holding cost formulations, without either example polluting the other’s
prompt context. Third, the knowledge base itself becomes an auditable
artifact: practitioners and researchers can inspect which examples were
retrieved for a given generation, providing a degree of transparency and
debuggability that is difficult to achieve with opaque monolithic
prompts.

However, building an effective RAG system for ORPilot also raises
several research questions worth investigating. The design of the
embedding space is particularly important: standard semantic similarity
over natural language descriptions may be insufficient to distinguish
structurally similar but semantically distinct optimization patterns;
embeddings that encode mathematical structure, e.g., constraint types,
variable domains, sparsity patterns, may be necessary for high-precision
retrieval. The construction and curation of the knowledge base also
requires care: examples must be verified correct, sufficiently diverse
to cover the problem space, and annotated with enough metadata to
support accurate retrieval. Finally, the interaction between retrieval
and in-context learning deserves study. The ordering, formatting, and
number of retrieved examples all influence generation quality, and
optimal retrieval strategies may differ between the IR generation and
code generation stages of the pipeline.

## Appendix C Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")

import gurobipy as gp

from gurobipy import GRB

def solve(data, time_limit=None, show_solver_log=False):

SEP = "\x1f"

\# Load all sets from sets.csv

sets_data = data\["sets"\]

production_sites = \[r\["element"\] for r in sets_data if
r\["set_name"\] == "production_sites"\]

distribution_centers = \[r\["element"\] for r in sets_data if
r\["set_name"\] == "distribution_centers"\]

customers = \[r\["element"\] for r in sets_data if r\["set_name"\] ==
"customers"\]

products = \[r\["element"\] for r in sets_data if r\["set_name"\] ==
"products"\]

periods = \[r\["element"\] for r in sets_data if r\["set_name"\] ==
"periods"\]

\# Load parameters with appropriate defaults

\# Demand: missing = 0

demand = {}

for r in data\["demand"\]:

key = (r\["customer_id"\], r\["product_id"\], r\["period"\])

demand\[key\] = float(r\["demand_quantity"\])

\# Production capacity: missing = unlimited

prod_cap = {}

for r in data\["production_capacity"\]:

key = (r\["site_id"\], r\["period"\])

prod_cap\[key\] = float(r\["capacity"\])

\# Storage capacities: missing = unlimited

storage_site = {}

for r in data\["storage_capacity_sites"\]:

storage_site\[r\["site_id"\]\] = float(r\["capacity"\])

storage_dc = {}

for r in data\["storage_capacity_dcs"\]:

storage_dc\[r\["dc_id"\]\] = float(r\["capacity"\])

\# Throughput capacity: missing = unlimited

throughput_cap = {}

for r in data\["throughput_capacity"\]:

key = (r\["dc_id"\], r\["period"\])

throughput_cap\[key\] = float(r\["capacity"\])

\# Production cost: missing = unavailable (inf)

prod_cost = {}

for r in data\["production_cost"\]:

key = (r\["site_id"\], r\["product_id"\])

prod_cost\[key\] = float(r\["unit_cost"\])

\# Transportation costs: missing = unavailable route

trans_cost_site_dc = {}

for r in data\["transport_cost_site_to_dc"\]:

key = (r\["from_site_id"\], r\["to_dc_id"\])

trans_cost_site_dc\[key\] = float(r\["unit_cost"\])

trans_cost_dc_cust = {}

for r in data\["transport_cost_dc_to_customer"\]:

key = (r\["from_dc_id"\], r\["to_customer_id"\])

trans_cost_dc_cust\[key\] = float(r\["unit_cost"\])

\# Holding costs: missing = 0

hold_cost_site = {}

for r in data\["holding_cost_sites"\]:

key = (r\["site_id"\], r\["product_id"\])

hold_cost_site\[key\] = float(r\["unit_cost"\])

hold_cost_dc = {}

for r in data\["holding_cost_dcs"\]:

key = (r\["dc_id"\], r\["product_id"\])

hold_cost_dc\[key\] = float(r\["unit_cost"\])

\# Revenue: missing = 0

revenue = {}

for r in data\["revenue"\]:

revenue\[r\["product_id"\]\] = float(r\["unit_revenue"\])

\# Create sets of valid connections (sparse network)

valid_site_dc = set(trans_cost_site_dc.keys())

valid_dc_cust = set(trans_cost_dc_cust.keys())

\# Build neighbor mappings for efficient constraint building

site_to_dc = {}

dc_from_site = {}

for i, j in valid_site_dc:

site_to_dc.setdefault(i, \[\]).append(j)

dc_from_site.setdefault(j, \[\]).append(i)

dc_to_cust = {}

cust_from_dc = {}

for j, c in valid_dc_cust:

dc_to_cust.setdefault(j, \[\]).append(c)

cust_from_dc.setdefault(c, \[\]).append(j)

\# Initialize model

env = gp.Env(empty=True)

env.setParam("LogToConsole", 1 if show_solver_log else 0)

env.start()

m = gp.Model(env=env)

if time_limit is not None:

m.Params.TimeLimit = time_limit

\# Decision variables

production = {}

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

\# Only create variable if production cost is finite

if prod_cost.get((i, p), float(’inf’)) \< float(’inf’):

production\[i, p, t\] = m.addVar(

name=f"production_quantity{SEP}{i}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}",

lb=0.0

)

ship_site_dc = {}

for i, j in valid_site_dc:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

ship_site_dc\[i, j, p, t\] = m.addVar(

name=f"shipment_site_to_dc{SEP}{i}{SEP}{j}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}",

lb=0.0

)

ship_dc_cust = {}

for j, c in valid_dc_cust:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

ship_dc_cust\[j, c, p, t\] = m.addVar(

name=f"shipment_dc_to_customer{SEP}{j}{SEP}{c}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}",

lb=0.0

)

inv_site = {}

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

inv_site\[i, p, t\] = m.addVar(

name=f"inventory_site{SEP}{i}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}",

lb=0.0

)

inv_dc = {}

for j in distribution_centers:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

inv_dc\[j, p, t\] = m.addVar(

name=f"inventory_dc{SEP}{j}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}",

lb=0.0

)

m.update()

\# Objective: maximize total profit = revenue - costs

\# Revenue from met demand

revenue_terms = \[\]

for (c, p, t), d in demand.items():

\# Sum of shipments to customer c for product p in period t

\# Only include if there are valid DCs serving this customer

if c in cust_from_dc:

for j in cust_from_dc\[c\]:

if (j, c, p, t) in ship_dc_cust:

revenue_terms.append(revenue.get(p, 0.0) \* ship_dc_cust\[j, c, p, t\])

\# Production costs

prod_cost_terms = \[\]

for (i, p, t), var in production.items():

prod_cost_terms.append(prod_cost.get((i, p), float(’inf’)) \* var)

\# Transportation costs

trans_cost_terms = \[\]

for (i, j, p, t), var in ship_site_dc.items():

trans_cost_terms.append(trans_cost_site_dc.get((i, j), float(’inf’)) \*
var)

for (j, c, p, t), var in ship_dc_cust.items():

trans_cost_terms.append(trans_cost_dc_cust.get((j, c), float(’inf’)) \*
var)

\# Holding costs

hold_cost_terms = \[\]

for (i, p, t), var in inv_site.items():

hold_cost_terms.append(hold_cost_site.get((i, p), 0.0) \* var)

for (j, p, t), var in inv_dc.items():

hold_cost_terms.append(hold_cost_dc.get((j, p), 0.0) \* var)

m.setObjective(

gp.quicksum(revenue_terms) -

gp.quicksum(prod_cost_terms) -

gp.quicksum(trans_cost_terms) -

gp.quicksum(hold_cost_terms),

GRB.MAXIMIZE

)

\# Constraints

\# 1. Production capacity

for i in production_sites:

for t in periods:

cap = prod_cap.get((i, t), float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

prod_vars = \[\]

for p in products:

if (i, p, t) in production:

prod_vars.append(production\[i, p, t\])

if prod_vars:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(prod_vars) \<= cap, name=f"prod_cap\_{i}\_{t}")

\# 2. Site storage capacity

for i in production_sites:

cap = storage_site.get(i, float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

for t in periods:

inv_vars = \[\]

for p in products:

inv_vars.append(inv_site\[i, p, t\])

if inv_vars:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(inv_vars) \<= cap, name=f"store_site\_{i}\_{t}")

\# 3. DC storage capacity

for j in distribution_centers:

cap = storage_dc.get(j, float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

for t in periods:

inv_vars = \[\]

for p in products:

inv_vars.append(inv_dc\[j, p, t\])

if inv_vars:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(inv_vars) \<= cap, name=f"store_dc\_{j}\_{t}")

\# 4. DC throughput capacity

for j in distribution_centers:

for t in periods:

cap = throughput_cap.get((j, t), float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

ship_vars = \[\]

if j in dc_to_cust:

for c in dc_to_cust\[j\]:

for p in products:

ship_vars.append(ship_dc_cust\[j, c, p, t\])

if ship_vars:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(ship_vars) \<= cap,
name=f"throughput\_{j}\_{t}")

\# 5. Demand satisfaction (equality, always create even if demand is 0)

for c in customers:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

d = demand.get((c, p, t), 0.0)

ship_vars = \[\]

if c in cust_from_dc:

for j in cust_from_dc\[c\]:

if (j, c, p, t) in ship_dc_cust:

ship_vars.append(ship_dc_cust\[j, c, p, t\])

\# Always create constraint, even if d == 0

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(ship_vars) == d, name=f"demand\_{c}\_{p}\_{t}")

\# 6. Site inventory balance

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

for idx, t in enumerate(periods):

\# Initial inventory is 0

if idx == 0:

prev_inv = 0.0

else:

prev_t = periods\[idx - 1\]

prev_inv = inv_site\[i, p, prev_t\]

\# Production term (if variable exists)

prod_term = production.get((i, p, t), 0.0)

\# Outgoing shipments

out_ship = \[\]

if i in site_to_dc:

for j in site_to_dc\[i\]:

out_ship.append(ship_site_dc\[i, j, p, t\])

m.addConstr(

inv_site\[i, p, t\] == prev_inv + prod_term - gp.quicksum(out_ship),

name=f"balance_site\_{i}\_{p}\_{t}"

)

\# 7. DC inventory balance

for j in distribution_centers:

for p in products:

for idx, t in enumerate(periods):

\# Initial inventory is 0

if idx == 0:

prev_inv = 0.0

else:

prev_t = periods\[idx - 1\]

prev_inv = inv_dc\[j, p, prev_t\]

\# Incoming shipments

in_ship = \[\]

if j in dc_from_site:

for i in dc_from_site\[j\]:

in_ship.append(ship_site_dc\[i, j, p, t\])

\# Outgoing shipments

out_ship = \[\]

if j in dc_to_cust:

for c in dc_to_cust\[j\]:

out_ship.append(ship_dc_cust\[j, c, p, t\])

m.addConstr(

inv_dc\[j, p, t\] == prev_inv + gp.quicksum(in_ship) -
gp.quicksum(out_ship),

name=f"balance_dc\_{j}\_{p}\_{t}"

)

\# Write LP file

try:

m.write("model.lp")

except Exception:

pass

\# Solve

m.optimize()

\# Process results

\_status_map = {

GRB.OPTIMAL: "optimal",

GRB.SUBOPTIMAL: "feasible",

GRB.INFEASIBLE: "infeasible",

GRB.UNBOUNDED: "unbounded",

}

status = \_status_map.get(m.Status, "error")

obj = None

variables = {}

if status in ("optimal", "feasible"):

obj = m.ObjVal

for v in m.getVars():

variables\[v.VarName\] = v.X

\# Group variables

\_groups = {}

for key, val in variables.items():

prefix = key.split(SEP, 1)\[0\] if SEP in key else key

\_groups.setdefault(prefix, {})\[key\] = val

\_dim_labels = {

"production_quantity": \["site_id", "product_id", "period"\],

"shipment_site_to_dc": \["from_site_id", "to_dc_id", "product_id",
"period"\],

"shipment_dc_to_customer": \["from_dc_id", "to_customer_id",
"product_id", "period"\],

"inventory_site": \["site_id", "product_id", "period"\],

"inventory_dc": \["dc_id", "product_id", "period"\],

}

variable_groups = \[

{

"group_name": g,

"dimension_labels": \_dim_labels.get(g, \[\]),

"variables": gvars

}

for g, gvars in \_groups.items()

\]

return {

"status": status,

"objective_value": obj,

"variables": variables,

"variable_groups": variable_groups

}

## Appendix D Solution Report Produced by Reporter Agent for Problem in Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization (Pure LP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")

Multi-period Multi-product Profit Maximization

1.  1.
    Executive Summary

    The optimization model successfully determined the maximum-profit
    operating plan for a supply chain network spanning 50 production
    sites, 50 distribution centers, 500 customers, and 500 products over
    12 monthly periods. The solver found a provably optimal solution
    with a total network profit of \$155,729,604.44.

    All 500 customers are fully served across every product and period.
    The plan achieves this by activating 41 of the 50 available
    production sites and routing goods through 48 of the 50 distribution
    centers, using 197 distinct site-to-DC shipping lanes.
2.  2.
    Key Decisions

    - •
      Production

      Total production across the planning horizon is approximately 5.42
      million units. Production ramps up steadily through the year,
      peaking in Period 12 (520,674 units), which suggests that
      late-period demand or favorable economics drive maximum output
      toward year-end.

      | Period | Total Production (units) |
      |--------|--------------------------|
      | 1      | 387,420                  |
      | 2      | 378,164                  |
      | 3      | 411,817                  |
      | 4      | 444,224                  |
      | 5      | 456,138                  |
      | 6      | 471,652                  |
      | 7      | 490,375                  |
      | 8      | 478,568                  |
      | 9      | 463,644                  |
      | 10     | 456,197                  |
      | 11     | 458,481                  |
      | 12     | 520,674                  |

      The top five production sites by total output are:

      | Site   | Total Output (units) |
      |--------|----------------------|
      | PS_017 | 514,334              |
      | PS_036 | 494,114              |
      | PS_050 | 490,157              |
      | PS_042 | 379,648              |
      | PS_024 | 263,380              |
    - •
      Facility Utilization

      - –
        9 production sites are idle throughout the entire planning
        horizon: PS_003, PS_008, PS_011, PS_030, PS_038, PS_039, PS_040,
        PS_041, and PS_047. These sites are either more expensive to
        operate, have lower capacity, or serve market areas that are
        better covered by nearby active sites.
      - –
        2 distribution centers are unused: DC_001 and DC_042. All other
        48 DCs participate in fulfilling customer demand.
    - •
      Distribution

      The network ships goods through 197 distinct production site-to-DC
      lane combinations. The top five DCs by throughput volume are:

      | DC     | Total Volume (units) |
      |--------|----------------------|
      | DC_024 | 664,979              |
      | DC_025 | 259,758              |
      | DC_028 | 240,684              |
      | DC_030 | 219,501              |
      | DC_038 | 202,703              |

      DC_024 handles roughly 12% of total network volume, making it a
      critical node. Any disruption to this facility would have an
      outsized impact on service levels.
    - •
      Inventory

      The plan uses inventory as a buffer, building stock in mid-year
      periods and drawing it down toward year-end. Both production sites
      and DCs follow a similar seasonal pattern:

      |        |                        |                      |
      |--------|------------------------|----------------------|
      | Period | Site Inventory (units) | DC Inventory (units) |
      | 1      | 3,606                  | 8,474                |
      | 2      | 8,112                  | 28,640               |
      | 3      | 10,577                 | 39,579               |
      | 4      | 11,763                 | 40,142               |
      | 5      | 9,719                  | 34,606               |
      | 6      | 7,404                  | 22,214               |
      | 7      | 2,267                  | 9,283                |
      | 8      | 358                    | 2,807                |
      | 9      | 286                    | 2,011                |
      | 10     | 2,154                  | 13,958               |
      | 11     | 9,591                  | 44,449               |
      | 12     | 0                      | 0                    |

      Inventory peaks at 40,142 units across DCs in Period 4, then
      declines sharply. The DC inventory spike in Period 11 (44,449
      units) followed by a full drawdown in Period 12 indicates the
      model is pre-positioning stock to meet high late-year demand. Zero
      ending inventory in Period 12 is expected behavior for a
      finite-horizon model: the solver correctly avoids carrying unsold
      stock past the planning window.
3.  3.
    Notable Findings and Concerns

    - •
      9 idle production sites: Nearly 18% of production capacity is left
      unused. Before removing these sites from the network or reducing
      their capacity, it is worth investigating whether they become
      active under different demand scenarios or cost structures. They
      may serve as surge capacity.
    - •
      DC_024 concentration risk: A single DC handles 12% of all
      deliveries. If this center faces disruption (weather, labor,
      capacity ceiling), a large portion of the customer base is
      affected. A sensitivity run that caps DC_024 throughput would
      reveal how much profit is lost and which alternative routes the
      network would use.
    - •
      Mid-year inventory build-up: Holding inventory for 3–4 periods
      adds holding cost. If holding costs are high, a solution with
      smoother production and lower peak inventory may be preferable
      even at a small reduction in revenue. A multi-objective run or an
      added constraint on maximum inventory level would surface this
      trade-off.
    - •
      End-of-horizon effect: Zero inventory in Period 12 is
      mathematically optimal for this model but may leave the business
      exposed if demand continues into Period 13. Extending the planning
      horizon or adding a terminal inventory value would give a more
      realistic picture.
    - •
      Unused DCs (DC_001, DC_042): These facilities incur no shipping
      volume. If there are fixed operating costs not captured in this LP
      model (e.g., lease costs), their ongoing cost should be weighed
      against the value of having them available as backup capacity.
4.  4.
    Suggested Next Steps

    - •
      Sensitivity analysis on revenue and production cost: Small changes
      in unit revenue or production cost can shift which sites and DCs
      are active. Run a parametric sweep to identify the break-even cost
      at which the 9 idle sites become economical.
    - •
      Capacity tightening: Artificially reduce DC_024’s throughput cap
      to 80% of its current utilization and re-solve to understand the
      cost of concentration risk.
    - •
      Extend the horizon: Add a Period 13 or a terminal inventory value
      to eliminate the artificial drawdown effect and get a
      rolling-horizon plan.
    - •
      Add fixed costs: If opening or operating a site/DC incurs a fixed
      periodic cost, upgrade to a MIP model (as in the output_MIP_new
      scenario) to jointly optimize facility selection and flow
      decisions.
    - •
      Stochastic demand: Replace deterministic demand with scenarios to
      produce a robust plan that performs well even if demand deviates
      from forecast.
5.  5.
    Output Files

    - •
      solution_production_quantity.csv
      Records how many units of each product were produced at each
      production site in each period. Use this to schedule factory
      workloads — each row tells a site manager exactly what to produce
      in a given month.
      Columns: site_id (which production site), product_id (which
      product), period (month number), value (units to produce).
    - •
      solution_shipment_site_to_dc.csv
      Records the volume of each product shipped from each production
      site to each distribution center in each period. Use this to plan
      outbound logistics from factories — trucks, freight bookings, and
      warehouse receiving schedules at DCs.
      Columns: from_site_id (origin site), to_dc_id (destination DC),
      product_id, period, value (units shipped).
    - •
      solution_shipment_dc_to_customer.csv
      Records the volume of each product shipped from each DC to each
      customer in each period. This is the last-mile delivery plan — use
      it to generate pick-pack-ship orders and communicate delivery
      quantities to customers.
      Columns: from_dc_id (origin DC), to_customer_id (destination
      customer), product_id, period, value (units delivered).
    - •
      solution_inventory_site.csv
      Records the end-of-period inventory of each product held at each
      production site. Use this to plan warehouse space at factories and
      to verify that storage capacity constraints are not being
      violated.
      Columns: site_id, product_id, period, value (units in stock at end
      of period).
    - •
      solution_inventory_dc.csv
      Records the end-of-period inventory of each product held at each
      distribution center. Use this to manage DC storage space and to
      anticipate when inventory build-up is largest (Periods 3–4 and
      Period 11).
      Columns: dc_id, product_id, period, value (units in stock at end
      of period).

Structured Summary

1.  1.
    Objective:

    Maximize total profit over a 12-period (month) planning horizon.
    Profit is defined as: Total Revenue minus Total Cost.

    - •
      Revenue comes from selling products to customers.
    - •
      Cost includes:

      - –
        Production cost.
      - –
        Transportation cost (from production sites to distribution
        centers, and from distribution centers to customers).
      - –
        Inventory holding cost (at production sites and distribution
        centers).
      - –
        Facility opening and operating costs (for production sites and
        distribution centers).
2.  2.
    Decision Variables: The model will determine, for each product, time
    period, and relevant location:

    - •
      Production Quantity: How much of each product to produce at each
      production site in each period.
    - •
      Transportation Flow:

      - –
        Quantity shipped from each production site to each distribution
        center.
      - –
        Quantity shipped from each distribution center to each customer.
    - •
      Inventory Level: Amount of each product held in inventory at each
      production site and each distribution center at the end of each
      period.
    - •
      Facility Opening (Binary): Whether to open each potential
      production site and each potential distribution center in each
      period. Once opened, a facility remains open for all future
      periods.
3.  3.
    Constraints:

    - •
      Production Capacity: Production at each site in each period cannot
      exceed its capacity.
    - •
      Throughput Capacity: Total flow through each distribution center
      in each period cannot exceed its capacity.
    - •
      Storage Capacity: Inventory held at each production site and
      distribution center in each period cannot exceed its storage
      capacity.
    - •
      Demand Fulfillment: For each customer, product, and period, the
      total quantity shipped from all distribution centers must equal
      the demand.
    - •
      Logical / Linking Constraints:

      - –
        A production site can only produce if it is open in that period.
      - –
        A distribution center can only receive or ship goods if it is
        open in that period.
    - •
      Inventory Balance: For each product at each facility (production
      site and distribution center), the inflow plus previous inventory
      must equal the outflow plus current inventory in each period.
4.  4.
    Parameters (with Indices): The following data will be required,
    indexed by the relevant categories:

    - •
      Indices:

      - –
        i $`\in`$ Set of potential production sites.
      - –
        j $`\in`$ Set of potential distribution centers.
      - –
        k $`\in`$ Set of potential customers.
      - –
        p $`\in`$ Set of products.
      - –
        t $`\in`$ Set of time periods (1..12).
    - •
      Parameters:

      - –
        demand\[k, p, t\]: Demand for product p from customer k in
        period t.
      - –
        production_capacity\[i, p, t\] (or \[i, t\] if shared): Capacity
        for producing product p at site i in period t.
      - –
        throughput_capacity\[j, t\]: Handling capacity at distribution
        center j in period t.
      - –
        storage_capacity\[i, t\]: Inventory storage capacity at
        production site i in period t.
      - –
        storage_capacity\[j, t\]: Inventory storage capacity at
        distribution center j in period t.
      - –
        production_cost\[i, p, t\]: Unit cost to produce product p at
        site i in period t.
      - –
        transport_cost_prod_to_dc\[i, j, p, t\]: Unit cost to ship
        product p from site i to DC j in period t.
      - –
        transport_cost_dc_to_cust\[j, k, p, t\]: Unit cost to ship
        product p from DC j to customer k in period t.
      - –
        holding_cost_site\[i, p, t\]: Unit cost to hold one unit of
        product p in inventory at site i at the end of period t.
      - –
        holding_cost_dc\[j, p, t\]: Unit cost to hold one unit of
        product p in inventory at DC j at the end of period t.
      - –
        fixed_cost_open_site\[i, t\]: One-time fixed cost to open
        production site i in period t.
      - –
        fixed_cost_open_dc\[j, t\]: One-time fixed cost to open
        distribution center j in period t.
      - –
        operating_cost_site\[i, t\]: Fixed operating cost for production
        site i if it is open in period t.
      - –
        operating_cost_dc\[j, t\]: Fixed operating cost for distribution
        center j if it is open in period t.
      - –
        revenue\[p, k, t\]: Unit revenue from selling product p to
        customer k in period t.

Structured Summary (Revised)

1.  1.
    Objective:

    Maximize total profit over a 12-period (month) planning horizon.
    Profit = Total Revenue $`-`$ Total Cost.

    - •
      Revenue: From selling products to customers.
    - •
      Cost Components:

      - –
        Production cost.
      - –
        Transportation cost (two legs: production sites $`\rightarrow`$
        distribution centers, and distribution centers $`\rightarrow`$
        customers).
      - –
        Inventory holding cost (at production sites and distribution
        centers).
      - –
        Fixed costs for opening and operating facilities.
2.  2.
    Decision Variables:

    For each product p, time period t (1..12), and relevant locations:

    - •
      Production Quantity: Amount of product p produced at production
      site i in period t.
    - •
      Transportation Flow:

      - –
        Quantity of product p shipped from production site i to
        distribution center j in period t.
      - –
        Quantity of product p shipped from distribution center j to
        customer k in period t.
    - •
      Inventory Level: Amount of product p held at the end of period t
      at production site i and at distribution center j.
    - •
      Facility Opening (Binary): Whether to open production site i in
      period t, and whether to open distribution center j in period t.
      Once opened, a facility remains open for all subsequent periods.
3.  3.
    Constraints:

    - •
      Production Capacity: For each site i and period t, total
      production (across all products) $`\leq`$ production_capacity\[i,
      t\].
    - •
      Throughput Capacity: For each distribution center j and period t,
      total outbound flow (to all customers, for all products) $`\leq`$
      throughput_capacity\[j, t\].
    - •
      Storage Capacity: For each production site i, inventory (across
      all products) at the end of any period $`\leq`$
      storage_capacity\[i\]. Similarly for each distribution center j
      with its own storage_capacity\[j\].
    - •
      Demand Fulfillment: For each customer k, product p, and period t,
      the total quantity shipped from all distribution centers must
      equal demand\[k, p, t\].
    - •
      Logical / Linking Constraints:

      - –
        Production at a site i in period t can only be positive if the
        site is open in that period.
      - –
        A distribution center j can only have positive inbound or
        outbound flow in period t if it is open in that period.
    - •
      Inventory Balance: For each product p, facility (site i or DC j),
      and period t: Inventory($`t-1`$) + Inflow($`t`$) =
      Outflow($`t`$) + Inventory($`t`$).
4.  4.
    Parameters (with Indices):

    - •
      Indices:

      - –
        i $`\in`$ Set of potential production sites.
      - –
        j $`\in`$ Set of potential distribution centers.
      - –
        k $`\in`$ Set of customers.
      - –
        p $`\in`$ Set of products.
      - –
        t $`\in`$ Set of time periods (1..12).
    - •
      Parameters:

      - –
        demand\[k, p, t\]
      - –
        production_capacity\[i, t\] (shared by all products,
        time-dependent)
      - –
        throughput_capacity\[j, t\] (applied to total outbound flow,
        time-dependent)
      - –
        storage_capacity\[i\] (for production sites, time-invariant)
      - –
        storage_capacity\[j\] (for distribution centers, time-invariant)
      - –
        production_cost\[i, p\] (time-invariant)
      - –
        transport_cost_prod_to_dc\[i, j\] (product- and time-invariant)
      - –
        transport_cost_dc_to_cust\[j, k\] (product- and time-invariant)
      - –
        holding_cost_site\[i, p\] (time-invariant)
      - –
        holding_cost_dc\[j, p\] (time-invariant)
      - –
        fixed_cost_open_site\[i\] (one-time cost, incurred when opened,

      - –
        fixed_cost_open_dc\[j\] (one-time cost, incurred when opened,
        time-invariant)
      - –
        operating_cost_site\[i\] (incurred each period the site is open,

      - –
        operating_cost_dc\[j\] (incurred each period the DC is open,
        time-invariant per period)
      - –
        revenue\[p\] (per unit, customer- and time-invariant)

      Default: If omitted, the initial inventory is assumed to be 0 for
      all site–product pairs.
18. 18.
    initial_inventory_dcs.csv (Optional)

    - •
      Description: Initial inventory level for each product at each
      distribution center at the start of period 1 (before any inbound
      flows or shipments).
    - •
      Schema:

      - –
        dc_id (str): Must match an element with set_name =
        distribution_centers in sets.csv.
      - –
        product_id (str): Must match an element with set_name = products
        in sets.csv.
      - –
        quantity (float): The initial inventory quantity.
    - •
      Default: If omitted, the initial inventory is assumed to be 0 for
      all DC–product pairs.

## Appendix H Generated Solver Code for Problem in Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization with Binary Decisions (MIP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

import gurobipy as gp

from gurobipy import GRB

def solve(data: dict\[str, list\[dict\]\], time_limit: int \| None =
None, show_solver_log: bool = False) -\> dict:

SEP = "\x1f"

\# --- Load sets ---

production_sites = \[r\["element"\] for r in data\["sets"\] if
r\["set_name"\] == "production_sites"\]

distribution_centers = \[r\["element"\] for r in data\["sets"\] if
r\["set_name"\] == "distribution_centers"\]

customers = \[r\["element"\] for r in data\["sets"\] if r\["set_name"\]
== "customers"\]

products = \[r\["element"\] for r in data\["sets"\] if r\["set_name"\]
== "products"\]

periods = \[r\["element"\] for r in data\["sets"\] if r\["set_name"\] ==
"periods"\]

\# --- Load bigM ---

bigM = float(data\["bigM"\]\[0\]\["bigM"\])

\# --- Load parameters ---

production_cap = {(r\["site_id"\], str(r\["period_id"\])):

float(r\["capacity"\]) for r in data\["production_capacity"\]}

throughput_cap = {(r\["dc_id"\], str(r\["period_id"\])):

float(r\["capacity"\]) for r in data\["throughput_capacity"\]}

storage_cap_site = {r\["site_id"\]: float(r\["capacity"\]) for r in
data\["storage_capacity_sites"\]}

storage_cap_dc = {r\["dc_id"\]: float(r\["capacity"\]) for r in
data\["storage_capacity_dcs"\]}

production_cost = {(r\["site_id"\], r\["product_id"\]):
float(r\["unit_cost"\]) for r in data\["production_cost"\]}

transport_cost_pd = {(r\["site_id"\], r\["dc_id"\]):

float(r\["unit_cost"\]) for r in data\["transport_cost_prod_to_dc"\]}

transport_cost_dc = {(r\["dc_id"\], r\["customer_id"\]):

float(r\["unit_cost"\]) for r in data\["transport_cost_dc_to_cust"\]}

holding_cost_site = {(r\["site_id"\], r\["product_id"\]):
float(r\["unit_cost"\]) for r in data\["holding_cost_sites"\]}

holding_cost_dc = {(r\["dc_id"\], r\["product_id"\]):
float(r\["unit_cost"\]) for r in data\["holding_cost_dcs"\]}

fixed_cost_site = {r\["site_id"\]: float(r\["cost"\]) for r in
data\["fixed_cost_open_sites"\]}

fixed_cost_dc = {r\["dc_id"\]: float(r\["cost"\]) for r in
data\["fixed_cost_open_dcs"\]}

operating_cost_site = {r\["site_id"\]: float(r\["cost"\]) for r in
data\["operating_cost_sites"\]}

operating_cost_dc = {r\["dc_id"\]: float(r\["cost"\]) for r in
data\["operating_cost_dcs"\]}

revenue = {r\["product_id"\]: float(r\["unit_revenue"\]) for r in
data\["revenue"\]}

demand = {(r\["customer_id"\], r\["product_id"\],
str(r\["period_id"\])): float(r\["demand"\]) for r in data\["demand"\]}

init_inv_site = {(r\["site_id"\], r\["product_id"\]):

float(r\["quantity"\]) for r in data.get("initial_inventory_sites",
\[\])}

init_inv_dc = {(r\["dc_id"\], r\["product_id"\]):

float(r\["quantity"\]) for r in data.get("initial_inventory_dcs", \[\])}

\# --- Sparse links ---

prod_to_dc_links = set((r\["site_id"\], r\["dc_id"\]) for r in
data\["transport_cost_prod_to_dc"\])

dc_to_cust_links = set((r\["dc_id"\], r\["customer_id"\]) for r in
data\["transport_cost_dc_to_cust"\])

\# --- Build model ---

env = gp.Env(empty=True)

env.setParam("LogToConsole", 1 if show_solver_log else 0)

env.start()

m = gp.Model(env=env)

if time_limit is not None:

m.Params.TimeLimit = time_limit

\# --- Decision variables ---

\# Production

prod = {}

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

if (i, p) in production_cost:

for t in periods:

prod\[i, p, t\] = m.addVar(lb=0, name=f"prod{SEP}{i}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}")

\# Flow prod -\> dc

flow_pd = {}

for (i, j) in prod_to_dc_links:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

flow_pd\[i, j, p, t\] = m.addVar(lb=0,
name=f"flow_pd{SEP}{i}{SEP}{j}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}")

\# Flow dc -\> cust

flow_dc = {}

for (j, k) in dc_to_cust_links:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

flow_dc\[j, k, p, t\] = m.addVar(lb=0,
name=f"flow_dc{SEP}{j}{SEP}{k}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}")

\# Inventory at sites

inv_site = {}

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

inv_site\[i, p, t\] = m.addVar(lb=0,
name=f"inv_site{SEP}{i}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}")

\# Inventory at DCs

inv_dc = {}

for j in distribution_centers:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

inv_dc\[j, p, t\] = m.addVar(lb=0,
name=f"inv_dc{SEP}{j}{SEP}{p}{SEP}{t}")

\# Binary open variables

open_site = {}

for i in production_sites:

for t in periods:

open_site\[i, t\] = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY,
name=f"open_site{SEP}{i}{SEP}{t}")

open_dc = {}

for j in distribution_centers:

for t in periods:

open_dc\[j, t\] = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY,
name=f"open_dc{SEP}{j}{SEP}{t}")

m.update()

\# --- Objective ---

obj = gp.LinExpr()

\# Revenue

for (j, k) in dc_to_cust_links:

for p in products:

rev_p = revenue.get(p, 0.0)

for t in periods:

obj += rev_p \* flow_dc\[j, k, p, t\]

\# Production cost

for (i, p, t), var in prod.items():

obj -= production_cost.get((i, p), 0.0) \* var

\# Transport cost prod -\> dc

for (i, j, p, t), var in flow_pd.items():

obj -= transport_cost_pd.get((i, j), 0.0) \* var

\# Transport cost dc -\> cust

for (j, k, p, t), var in flow_dc.items():

obj -= transport_cost_dc.get((j, k), 0.0) \* var

\# Holding cost sites

for (i, p, t), var in inv_site.items():

obj -= holding_cost_site.get((i, p), 0.0) \* var

\# Holding cost dcs

for (j, p, t), var in inv_dc.items():

obj -= holding_cost_dc.get((j, p), 0.0) \* var

\# Fixed opening cost (incurred when first opened = first period
open_site\[i,t\]=1)

\# Fixed cost when opened: open_site\[i,t\] - open_site\[i,t-1\] = 1

\# Use auxiliary: open_site is monotone, so fixed_cost \* open_site\[i,
first_t\] captures opening cost

\# Actually: fixed cost incurred once = fixed_cost \*
(open_site\[i,t\] - open_site\[i,t-1\]) summed over t

\# = fixed_cost \* open_site\[i, last_period\] (because telescoping =
open_site at last period since initial=0)

\# But simpler: add fixed_cost \* open_site\[i,t\] contribution for
first period minus previous

\# We’ll model as: sum_t (open_site\[i,t\] - open_site\[i,t-1\]) \*
fixed_cost

\# which equals fixed_cost \* open_site\[i, last_t\] since
open_site\[i,0\]=0

\# Better to keep it explicit in the loop for correctness with monotone
constraint

sorted_periods = periods \# already in order from sets

for i in production_sites:

fc = fixed_cost_site.get(i, 0.0)

oc = operating_cost_site.get(i, 0.0)

for idx, t in enumerate(sorted_periods):

\# Operating cost per period open

obj -= oc \* open_site\[i, t\]

\# Fixed opening cost: incurred when opened (first period with open=1)

if idx == 0:

obj -= fc \* open_site\[i, t\]

else:

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

obj -= fc \* (open_site\[i, t\] - open_site\[i, t_prev\])

for j in distribution_centers:

fc = fixed_cost_dc.get(j, 0.0)

oc = operating_cost_dc.get(j, 0.0)

for idx, t in enumerate(sorted_periods):

obj -= oc \* open_dc\[j, t\]

if idx == 0:

obj -= fc \* open_dc\[j, t\]

else:

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

obj -= fc \* (open_dc\[j, t\] - open_dc\[j, t_prev\])

m.setObjective(obj, GRB.MAXIMIZE)

\# --- Constraints ---

\# Production capacity

for i in production_sites:

for t in periods:

cap = production_cap.get((i, t), float(’inf’))

prods_it = \[prod\[i, p, t\] for p in products if (i, p, t) in prod\]

if prods_it and cap \< float(’inf’):

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(prods_it) \<= cap \* open_site\[i, t\],

name=f"prod_cap\_{i}\_{t}")

elif prods_it:

\# unlimited capacity but still tied to open

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(prods_it) \<= bigM \* open_site\[i, t\],

name=f"prod_cap\_{i}\_{t}")

\# Throughput capacity (outbound from DC)

for j in distribution_centers:

for t in periods:

cap = throughput_cap.get((j, t), float(’inf’))

flows_jt = \[flow_dc\[j, k, p, t\] for (jj, k) in dc_to_cust_links if jj
== j

for p in products if (j, k, p, t) in flow_dc\]

if flows_jt:

if cap \< float(’inf’):

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(flows_jt) \<= cap \* open_dc\[j, t\],

name=f"throughput\_{j}\_{t}")

else:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(flows_jt) \<= bigM \* open_dc\[j, t\],

name=f"throughput\_{j}\_{t}")

\# Storage capacity sites

for i in production_sites:

cap = storage_cap_site.get(i, float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

for t in periods:

inv_it = \[inv_site\[i, p, t\] for p in products if (i, p, t) in
inv_site\]

if inv_it:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(inv_it) \<= cap, name=f"storage_site\_{i}\_{t}")

\# Storage capacity DCs

for j in distribution_centers:

cap = storage_cap_dc.get(j, float(’inf’))

if cap \< float(’inf’):

for t in periods:

inv_jt = \[inv_dc\[j, p, t\] for p in products if (j, p, t) in inv_dc\]

if inv_jt:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(inv_jt) \<= cap, name=f"storage_dc\_{j}\_{t}")

\# Inbound flow to DC tied to open_dc

for j in distribution_centers:

for t in periods:

flows_in = \[flow_pd\[i, j, p, t\] for (ii, jj) in prod_to_dc_links if
jj == j

for i in \[ii\] for p in products if (i, j, p, t) in flow_pd\]

if flows_in:

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(flows_in) \<= bigM \* open_dc\[j, t\],

name=f"dc_open_inflow\_{j}\_{t}")

\# Demand fulfillment

for k in customers:

for p in products:

for t in periods:

d = demand.get((k, p, t), 0.0)

\# rebuild properly

flows = \[flow_dc\[j, k, p, t\] for j in distribution_centers

if (j, k) in dc_to_cust_links and (j, k, p, t) in flow_dc\]

m.addConstr(gp.quicksum(flows) == d, name=f"demand\_{k}\_{p}\_{t}")

\# Monotone opening: once open, stays open

for i in production_sites:

for idx in range(1, len(sorted_periods)):

t = sorted_periods\[idx\]

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

m.addConstr(open_site\[i, t\] \>= open_site\[i, t_prev\],

name=f"mono_site\_{i}\_{t}")

for j in distribution_centers:

for idx in range(1, len(sorted_periods)):

t = sorted_periods\[idx\]

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

m.addConstr(open_dc\[j, t\] \>= open_dc\[j, t_prev\],

name=f"mono_dc\_{j}\_{t}")

\# Inventory balance at production sites

for i in production_sites:

for p in products:

for idx, t in enumerate(sorted_periods):

\# inbound: production

prod_var = prod.get((i, p, t))

\# outbound: flows to DCs

flows_out = \[flow_pd\[i, j, p, t\] for (ii, j) in prod_to_dc_links

if ii == i and (i, j, p, t) in flow_pd\]

\# current inventory

inv_cur = inv_site.get((i, p, t))

\# previous inventory

if idx == 0:

inv_prev_val = init_inv_site.get((i, p), 0.0)

lhs = gp.LinExpr(inv_prev_val)

else:

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

inv_prev = inv_site.get((i, p, t_prev))

lhs = gp.LinExpr()

if inv_prev is not None:

lhs += inv_prev

if prod_var is not None:

lhs += prod_var

rhs = gp.LinExpr()

if inv_cur is not None:

rhs += inv_cur

for fv in flows_out:

rhs += fv

m.addConstr(lhs == rhs, name=f"inv_bal_site\_{i}\_{p}\_{t}")

\# Inventory balance at distribution centers

for j in distribution_centers:

for p in products:

for idx, t in enumerate(sorted_periods):

\# inbound flows from production sites

flows_in = \[flow_pd\[i, j, p, t\] for (i, jj) in prod_to_dc_links

if jj == j and (i, j, p, t) in flow_pd\]

\# outbound flows to customers

flows_out = \[flow_dc\[j, k, p, t\] for (jj, k) in dc_to_cust_links

if jj == j and (j, k, p, t) in flow_dc\]

\# current inventory

inv_cur = inv_dc.get((j, p, t))

\# previous inventory

if idx == 0:

inv_prev_val = init_inv_dc.get((j, p), 0.0)

lhs = gp.LinExpr(inv_prev_val)

else:

t_prev = sorted_periods\[idx - 1\]

inv_prev = inv_dc.get((j, p, t_prev))

lhs = gp.LinExpr()

if inv_prev is not None:

lhs += inv_prev

for fv in flows_in:

lhs += fv

rhs = gp.LinExpr()

if inv_cur is not None:

rhs += inv_cur

for fv in flows_out:

rhs += fv

m.addConstr(lhs == rhs, name=f"inv_bal_dc\_{j}\_{p}\_{t}")

\# --- Write and optimize ---

try:

m.write("model.lp")

except Exception:

pass

m.optimize()

\_status_map = {

GRB.OPTIMAL: "optimal",

GRB.SUBOPTIMAL: "feasible",

GRB.INFEASIBLE: "infeasible",

GRB.UNBOUNDED: "unbounded",

}

status = \_status_map.get(m.Status, "error")

obj_val = m.ObjVal if m.Status in (GRB.OPTIMAL, GRB.SUBOPTIMAL) else
None

variables = {v.VarName: v.X for v in m.getVars()} if status in
("optimal", "feasible") else {}

\# --- Build variable groups ---

\_groups = {}

for key, val in variables.items():

prefix = key.split(SEP, 1)\[0\] if SEP in key else key

\_groups.setdefault(prefix, {})\[key\] = val

\_dim_labels = {

"prod": \["site_id", "product_id", "period_id"\],

"flow_pd": \["site_id", "dc_id", "product_id", "period_id"\],

"flow_dc": \["dc_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "period_id"\],

"inv_site": \["site_id", "product_id", "period_id"\],

"inv_dc": \["dc_id", "product_id", "period_id"\],

"open_site": \["site_id", "period_id"\],

"open_dc": \["dc_id", "period_id"\],

}

variable_groups = \[

{"group_name": g, "dimension_labels": \_dim_labels.get(g, \[\]),
"variables": gvars}

for g, gvars in \_groups.items()

\]

return {

"status": status,

"objective_value": obj_val,

"variables": variables,

"variable_groups": variable_groups,

}

## Appendix I Solution Report for Problem in Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Large-Scale Supply Chain Network Optimization with Binary Decisions (MIP) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ORPilot: A Production-Oriented Agentic LLM-for-OR Tool for Optimization Modeling")

Multi-period Facility Opening and Flow Optimization

1.  1.
    Executive Summary

    The optimization model determined the maximum-profit network design
    and operating plan for a supply chain spanning 25 candidate
    production sites, 25 distribution centers, 250 customers, and 500
    products over 12 monthly periods. The solver found a provably
    optimal solution with a total network profit of \$50,051,375.31.

    The model jointly decided which facilities to open and when, how
    much to produce at each site, and how to route goods to customers —
    all while accounting for fixed facility opening costs, per-period
    operating costs, production and transportation costs, and inventory
    holding costs. All 250 customers are fully served across every
    product and period.
2.  2.
    Facility Opening Decisions

    Production Sites

    The optimizer selected 13 of the 25 candidate production sites to
    open. Twelve sites open from the very first period; one site
    (PS_030) is held back until Period 7, representing a deliberate
    mid-year capacity expansion triggered by rising demand.

    - •
      Sites opened in Period 1 (12 sites): PS_013, PS_014, PS_017,
      PS_020, PS_021, PS_022, PS_024, PS_029, PS_035, PS_036, PS_042,
      PS_050
    - •
      Sites opened in Period 7 (1 site): PS_030
    - •
      Sites never opened (12 sites): PS_001, PS_003, PS_004, PS_005,
      PS_008, PS_015, PS_025, PS_039, PS_041, PS_044, PS_046, PS_047

    The 12 idle sites were not economical to open — their fixed opening
    costs, operating costs, or production costs were too high relative
    to the additional profit they would generate. Total fixed opening
    costs for the 13 opened sites amount to approximately \$6.3 million.

    Distribution Centers

    All 25 distribution centers are opened in Period 1. The optimizer
    determined it was profitable to activate the entire DC network from
    the start, paying a combined fixed opening cost of approximately
    \$7.4 million to ensure broad customer coverage throughout the
    planning horizon.
3.  3.
    Production Plan

    Total production across all 13 active sites and 12 periods is
    2,717,067 units — exactly matching total customer demand, confirming
    zero wasted production and full demand satisfaction.

    Production ramps up steadily through the year, peaking in Period 12:

    | Period | Total Production (units) |
    |--------|--------------------------|
    | 1      | 200,947                  |
    | 2      | 193,708                  |
    | 3      | 207,132                  |
    | 4      | 220,270                  |
    | 5      | 223,755                  |
    | 6      | 231,467                  |
    | 7      | 246,178                  |
    | 8      | 241,197                  |
    | 9      | 232,810                  |
    | 10     | 229,023                  |
    | 11     | 228,720                  |
    | 12     | 261,860                  |

    The jump in Period 7 (from 231,467 to 246,178) coincides precisely
    with PS_030 coming online, confirming that the mid-year opening is
    driven by a capacity need rather than cost savings alone.

    The top five production sites by total 12-month output are:

    | Site   | Total Output (units) |
    |--------|----------------------|
    | PS_050 | 400,717              |
    | PS_042 | 379,648              |
    | PS_024 | 263,380              |
    | PS_014 | 260,802              |
    | PS_036 | 233,349              |

    PS_050 and PS_042 together account for roughly 29% of total network
    production.
4.  4.
    Distribution

    Goods flow through 56 active production-site-to-DC lanes out of the
    full set of possible combinations. The top five distribution centers
    by total outbound volume are:

    | DC     | Total Volume (units) |
    |--------|----------------------|
    | DC_024 | 386,112              |
    | DC_004 | 155,628              |
    | DC_028 | 149,629              |
    | DC_025 | 146,516              |
    | DC_017 | 145,764              |

    DC_024 handles approximately 14% of all customer deliveries, making
    it the single most critical node in the network. The remaining 24
    DCs share the other 86% of volume.
5.  5.
    Inventory

    Both production sites and distribution centers carry stock across
    periods, with inventory peaking in the early-to-mid year before
    being drawn down toward zero by year-end.

    |        |                        |                      |
    |--------|------------------------|----------------------|
    | Period | Site Inventory (units) | DC Inventory (units) |
    | 1      | 3,929                  | 8,698                |
    | 2      | 8,841                  | 20,100               |
    | 3      | 12,201                 | 24,151               |
    | 4      | 13,037                 | 21,440               |
    | 5      | 9,593                  | 16,034               |
    | 6      | 6,977                  | 6,114                |
    | 7      | 1,551                  | 3,120                |
    | 8      | 57                     | 1,700                |
    | 9      | 0                      | 1,433                |
    | 10     | 1,909                  | 6,280                |
    | 11     | 10,737                 | 15,516               |
    | 12     | 0                      | 0                    |

    Site inventory peaks in Period 4 (13,037 units) and DC inventory
    peaks in Period 3 (24,151 units). Both decline sharply through
    mid-year, hitting near-zero by Periods 8–9. A secondary inventory
    build in Periods 10–11 pre-positions stock to fulfil the elevated
    Period 12 demand. Zero ending inventory across the entire network in
    Period 12 confirms the horizon-end drawdown is complete with no
    unsold stock.
6.  6.
    Notable Findings and Concerns

    - •
      12 idle production sites: Half of the candidate production network
      remains unopened. Before dismissing these sites, consider whether
      they would be activated under a demand increase scenario or if any
      of the opened sites face a disruption. They represent latent
      capacity that could be critical in contingency planning.
    - •
      PS_030 mid-year activation: The optimizer chose to defer opening
      PS_030 until Period 7 rather than open it in Period 1. This saves
      six months of fixed and operating costs. However, it means the
      network is running at tighter production capacity in the first
      half of the year. A sensitivity run could test whether moving the
      opening to Period 5 or 6 improves profit by reducing mid-year
      inventory build-up.
    - •
      DC_024 concentration risk: With 14% of all deliveries flowing
      through a single DC, any disruption to DC_024 would affect a large
      portion of the customer base. A scenario run capping DC_024’s
      throughput to 80% of current utilization would reveal the profit
      impact and identify which alternative DCs would absorb the
      overflow.
    - •
      Full DC network activation: Opening all 25 DCs from Period 1
      incurs ~\$7.4M in fixed costs immediately. If some DCs serve only
      a small number of customers, a variant model allowing DCs to open
      later (as with PS_030) might reduce early-period fixed cost
      outlay. The current formulation constrains DCs to open no later
      than the first period they handle flow — examining DC utilization
      rates would identify candidates for deferred opening.
    - •
      End-of-horizon inventory drawdown: Zero inventory at the end of
      Period 12 is optimal within the model but leaves no buffer if
      demand continues into Period 13. A rolling-horizon plan or a
      terminal inventory credit would produce more conservative
      end-state stock levels.
    - •
      Facility cost significance: Combined fixed opening costs for sites
      and DCs total approximately \$13.7 million — roughly 27% of the
      total net profit. Accurately estimating these one-time costs in
      the data is therefore critical; a 10% error in fixed costs shifts
      the reported profit by ~\$1.4M.
7.  7.
    Suggested Next Steps

    - •
      Deferred DC opening analysis: Relax the assumption that all DCs
      must open in Period 1. Allow DCs to open in any period and
      re-solve to test whether later openings for low-utilization DCs
      reduce total cost.
    - •
      PS_030 opening timing sensitivity: Test opening PS_030 in Periods
      5 and 6 to see if earlier activation reduces the inventory
      build-up in Periods 1–4 and improves overall profit.
    - •
      DC_024 stress test: Cap DC_024 throughput at 80% and re-solve to
      quantify concentration risk and identify which alternative DCs
      absorb the displaced volume.
    - •
      Idle site contingency value: Estimate the option value of the 12
      idle sites by solving a disruption scenario in which one or two
      opened sites become unavailable mid-horizon.
    - •
      LP relaxation comparison: Solving the LP relaxation (removing
      binary constraints) gives an upper bound on profit and reveals how
      much value is lost to the integrality requirement. A large gap
      suggests room to improve the formulation.
    - •
      Extend to a rolling horizon: Incorporate Period 13+ to eliminate
      end-of-horizon effects and generate a steady-state operating
      policy.
8.  8.
    Output Files

    - •
      solution_prod.csv
      Records how many units of each product were produced at each
      production site in each period. Only sites that were opened have
      non-zero production. Use this to schedule factory workloads month
      by month.
      Columns: site_id (which production site), product_id (which
      product), period_id (month 1–12), value (units produced).
    - •
      solution_flow_pd.csv
      Records the volume of each product shipped from each production
      site to each distribution center in each period. Use this to plan
      outbound factory logistics — freight bookings and DC receiving
      schedules.
      Columns: site_id (origin site), dc_id (destination DC),
      product_id, period_id, value (units shipped).
    - •
      solution_flow_dc.csv
      Records the volume of each product delivered from each DC to each
      customer in each period. This is the last-mile fulfillment plan —
      use it to generate customer delivery orders and communicate
      committed quantities.
      Columns: dc_id (origin DC), customer_id (destination customer),
      product_id, period_id, value (units delivered).
    - •
      solution_inv_site.csv
      Records the end-of-period inventory of each product held at each
      production site. Use this to manage warehouse space at factories
      and monitor storage capacity utilization, particularly in Periods
      3–4 when site stock is highest.
      Columns: site_id, product_id, period_id, value (units in stock at
      end of period).
    - •
      solution_inv_dc.csv
      Records the end-of-period inventory of each product held at each
      distribution center. Use this to manage DC warehouse space and
      plan receiving and putaway workloads — DC inventory peaks in
      Period 3.
      Columns: dc_id, product_id, period_id, value (units in stock at
      end of period).
    - •
      solution_open_site.csv
      Records the binary open/closed status of each production site in
      each period (1 = open, 0 = closed). Once a site opens it remains
      open for all subsequent periods (monotone constraint). Use this to
      plan staffing, utilities, and facility activation timelines.
      Columns: site_id, period_id, value (1 if open, 0 if closed).
    - •
      solution_open_dc.csv
      Records the binary open/closed status of each distribution center
      in each period. All 25 DCs are open from Period 1 onward. Use this
      to confirm DC activation schedules and cross-reference with lease
      and staffing plans.
      Columns: dc_id, period_id, value (1 if open, 0 if closed).
